#6706. The Best Oxford Shirt for Men in 2026, According to GQ

The story behind the Oxford shirt is a lot less thrilling than you’d expect. It didn’t earn that fancy-sounding sobriquet through some sacred connection to the tony British university; instead, the shirt's signature cotton fabric was just one of four named after a group of schools picked by a Scottish mill for their associations with society’s upper crust. (19th century marketing at its best!)

But of the quartet—the others were Harvard, Cambridge, and Yale, FYI—only the Oxford shirt achieved menswear icon status, becoming a quintessential emblem of American prep as a “sporting shirt” and then as a staple of casual attire. Nowadays, Oxford-cloth shirts come in every color imaginable, but none of ‘em look quite as classic as the OG—especially when they’re thoroughly worn-in and a little wrinkled. Below you’ll find 16 of our absolute favorites, each one more ready than the last to imbue your jeans, chinos, and trousers with the unmistakable swagger of adopted American royalty.

J.Crew’s Oxford shirts have been a staple of the catalog for decades and though its iconic Secret Wash shirts are the bestsellers of the bunch, we prefer its more recent release, the 1983 Oxford Shirt. It’s easy to miss the differences at a glance, yet the handful of subtle tweaks add up quick. First, the fit: a comfier, more relaxed silhouette that, despite its ‘80s reference, is spot on for 2027. Second, the fabric: a noticeably sturdier, heftier all-cotton Oxford that makes its best-selling Secret Wash shirts feel wimpy by comparison. Third, and most importantly, the collar: unlike its most popular shirts, the 1983 Oxford has a satisfyingly taller collar with a prep-approved collar roll. It gives the shirt more life and more nuance, but also looks great under a blazer.

If there’s any brand that could do the Oxford justice, it’s the British label, Drake’s, known for its none-too-posh take on all things tailoring. Its handsome entry into the Oxford shirt ring is a confluence of top-shelf materials and methodical construction, wrapped into a single shirt worth saving up for. Handmade in Somerset, England, Drake’s Oxford features single-needle construction with finished seams throughout, which takes the cut and sew process twice as long to complete—on top of the high-density stitching you’ll find throughout the shirt. Lustrous mother-of-pearl buttons make for a luxe upgrade while the collar—a button-down with a fabulous collar roll—is constructed with a floating interlining to give it a soft structure.

All in, Drake’s Oxford is what most other Oxfords aspire to be. And if you’re curious about what comes after J.Crew, this is your answer.

Wythe’s built its brand on western aesthetics with lasting quality—think properly-made cowboy boots, Yellowstone-worthy coats, and snap shirts. That the label would produce something as east-coast as an Oxford shirt is head-scratching. And yet, it’s one of the best versions we’ve tried. That’s because Wythe takes the same sort of rigor that it uses for its western and workwear garments and applies it to the preppy classic. This as close as anyone can get to a deadstock Oxford shirt plucked from a long-forgotten storage room. From the box pleat and locker loop to the unstructured long-point button-down collar, size-stamped collar stand and nostalgic paper packaging, it’s a good reminder of why prep in the ‘60s was so, so good.

Plain Oxford shirts too simple for your liking? Thom Browne's take isn’t overtly avant-garde, but it does boast a striped grosgrain placket that shows itself when you undo the top or bottom buttons, a stitched-on tag near the right hip, and a similarly striped locker loop beneath the collar. Each one is made in Italy from a soft, durable cotton fabric with noticeable cuffs and a sharply curved hem, making this iteration a better fit with sleek dress pants or even your most refined athleisure. (Talking to you, sneakers-with-suit crowd.)

This shirt won’t win you any browny points with the tailoring nerds, it will earn you cred with the fashion elite.

For the guy who’s quick to chat your ear off for 20 minutes when all you said was, “nice pants”, Jake’s is the go-to shirt whisperer. Jake’s began as founder Jake Wigham was amidst his studies at the London College of Fashion, honing his skills at a tailoring apprenticeship and fulfilling custom projects. It eventually blossomed into the talk of the menswear cognoscenti, who praised Wigham’s shirtmaking prowess. Each shirt is made-to-order, cut and sewn in the Jake’s studio by a small team of expert craftspeople, according to your specific measurements, with options for different collars, pockets, and fabrics. While we’ll always respect the old guard shirtmakers who’ve honed their style over generations, Jake’s bridges the gap between traditional craft and modern appeal—a Savile Row approach that speaks internet.

According to menswear lore, Brooks Brothers is responsible for bringing the Oxford shirt stateside. Quite a few decades later, everything’s still here, from the telltale collar to the button cuffs, patch pockets, and curved hems. One note: Brooks Brothers says it’s a ‘regular fit’, but there’s a bit more room in the chest than some of its counterparts.

Japan's obsession with Americana often comes full circle, as is the case with Kamakura. Its shirts are the envy of so many labels for its craftsmanship which parallels that of custom shirtmakers. We're talking mother-of-pearl buttons, high-density stitching, and major attention to minor details like the roll of the collar and single-needle seams.

Gitman Vintage's stateside-produced shirts have been a fixture of tasteful menswear shops for years not only for its high quality control, but for its tailored silhouettes and idiosyncratic details like chalk buttons, its signature contrasting horizontal bottom button hole, and soft collars.

J.Press's take on the Oxford shirt stands out as among the preppiest examples. Not only does it come from the storied uniform supplier of Yale's student body, but the perfectly rolled collar and flap chest pocket details give it a distinctly collegiate look that would pass muster on any Ivy League campus.

The Clark shirt is one of Proper Cloth's best selling shirts thanks to its beefy Oxford cloth material, bewilderingly good construction (felled seams, split yoke, unfused placket, shanked buttons), and near-perfect fit. For $125, you cannot get a better Oxford shirt. But you have to be willing to wait because every shirt is made to order and will take a couple weeks to get to you. If you can remember to think ahead and have some patience, it’s well worth the wait.

Swedish brand Rubato crafts its R Oxford less traditionally, but it’s no less an Oxford because of it. It might eschew the conventional button-down collar, but thanks its super-tight blue stripes, button cuffs, and a fitted body designed to look good tucked or untucked, it skews decidedly old-world. The real clincher though, is the fabric, a 100% Sea Island cotton so soft we keep trying to pet our computer screen.

With a nerd-satisfying 22 stitches per inch, troca shell buttons, and other refined details, you’d be forgiven for thinking this shirt was made on Jermyn Street, famed for its shirtmaking history. But Sid’s shirts are proudly made in Honduras which makes them a great value compared to the British alternative.

Todd Snyder's lightweight Oxford shirt takes the OG and makes it even more casual, a perfect piece for layering over a graphic tee thanks to its relaxed fit and feather-light cotton fabric.

The quality of an Oxford shirt comes down to the fabric, construction, fit, and collar. They’re a distinct kind of button-up that warrants its own buying guide separate from dress shirts. Why? There’s so much history behind the style and the fabric.

Oxford cloth is beefier than a typical dress shirt fabric with more texture and thus has a more casual quality befitting of rumpled chinos and sneakers, territory most dress shirt fabrics would feel absolutely out of place. Seph Skerritt, CEO of Proper Cloth, says “You can think of it as a tougher, more durable and more casual cousin to the pinpoint dress shirt.” The cotton yarns are thicker than broadcloth, twill, and poplin, so the hand is noticeably less fine. The heftier material means a high-quality Oxford cloth is more durable and can even last as long as a decade.

Construction-wise, you should typically look for the same sort of details as you would with other dress shirts. Clean stitches, felled seams, buttons properly sewn with shanks, and reinforced at the side seams. High-quality Oxford shirts will also feature a split yoke which is the panel that spans the shoulders and is cut on the bias to give the area natural stretch for ease of motion.

Fit is subjective, of course, but you want to make sure that the shoulder seams line up with your natural shoulders, if not a little below for a relaxed fit. The chest shouldn’t pull, but shouldn’t feel like a potato sack. As for the body, this is more or less subjective and delves into the kind of silhouette you’re after, but if the fabric is pulling around the buttons, your shirt is too tight. And, depending on whether you like to tuck, should be long enough.

Oxford cloth shirts can come in any variety of collars, but the most common are button-down, spread, and point collars. Big menswear nerds will obsess over finding the perfect collar roll, a detail found in the golden age of Ivy style by the likes of Brooks Brothers and J.Press.

Oxford shirts are near and dear to our hearts. They’re classic, versatile, and durable—true staples that every guy should have. So we had opinions on what we wanted out of them. It all starts with the star of the show—the titular fabric. The Oxford cloth has to be meatier than the average dress shirt and with some noticeable texture. They should ideally be able to rumple more than crease and wrinkle.

From there, we looked for Oxfords that are well-constructed with beautiful buttons and, crucially, handsome collars. And because you can be surprised no matter how much you’re paying, we looked at Oxfords in all price points to find the best ones regardless of the tag.

So we looked to the seasoned veterans that built the Oxford’s reputation as well as the newcomers that are pushing it into the 21st-century as well as the runway designers that have let their imaginations run wild.

Style is subjective, we know—that’s the fun of it. But we’re serious about helping our audience get dressed. Whether it’s the best white sneakers, the flyest affordable suits, or the need-to-know menswear drops of the week, GQ Recommends’ perspective is built on years of hands-on experience, an insider awareness of what’s in and what’s next, and a mission to find the best version of everything out there, at every price point.

Our staffers aren’t able to try on every single piece of clothing you read about on GQ.com (fashion moves fast these days), but we have an intimate knowledge of each brand’s strengths and know the hallmarks of quality clothing—from materials and sourcing, to craftsmanship, to sustainability efforts that aren’t just greenwashing. GQ Recommends heavily emphasizes our own editorial experience with those brands, how they make their clothes, and how those clothes have been reviewed by customers. Bottom line: GQ wouldn’t tell you to wear it if we wouldn’t.

We make every effort to cast as wide of a net as possible, with an eye on identifying the best options across three key categories: quality, fit, and price.

To kick off the process, we enlist the GQ Recommends braintrust to vote on our contenders. Some of the folks involved have worked in retail, slinging clothes to the masses; others have toiled for small-batch menswear labels; all spend way too much time thinking about what hangs in their closets.

We lean on that collective experience to guide our search, culling a mix of household names, indie favorites, and the artisanal imprints on the bleeding-edge of the genre. Then we narrow down the assortment to the picks that scored the highest across quality, fit, and price.

Across the majority of our buying guides, our team boasts firsthand experience with the bulk of our selects, but a handful are totally new to us. So after several months of intense debate, we tally the votes, collate the anecdotal evidence, and emerge with a list of what we believe to be the absolute best of the category right now, from the tried-and-true stalwarts to the modern disruptors, the affordable beaters to the wildly expensive (but wildly worth-it) designer riffs.

Whatever your preferences, whatever your style, there's bound to be a superlative version on this list for you. (Read more about GQ's testing process here.)

#6705. Hugo Boss CEO Daniel Grieder Steps Down Amid Frasers Takeover

Hugo Boss has announced that CEO Daniel Grieder will depart the German company, effective December 31. David Epstein — currently the chief brand partnerships officer at Frasers Group — will replace him, effective January 1, 2027.

Grieder was appointed CEO in June 2021, overseeing the company’s Claim 5 turnaround — a strategy focused on improving brand relevance, product innovation, digital output, omnichannel experience, and operational logistics to drive growth. Before Hugo Boss, Grieder spent more than 20 years at Tommy Hilfiger.

His mandate at Hugo Boss was to double company sales to €4 billion by 2025, believing the company had lost its relevance within the fashion space. He decided that while the brand’s heritage remained strong, it needed reframing. In 2022, he divided the parent company into two individual brands: Hugo and Boss — positioning Hugo for Gen Z and Boss for millennials.

Grieder also ushered in an ongoing collaboration with David Beckham, introduced in 2025 as a co-designed capsule. For fiscal 2025, Hugo Boss reported €4.3 billion in group sales.

“Looking back, what makes me proudest is what our teams accomplished over the past years,” said Grieder in a statement. “Together, we have brought Boss and Hugo back on stage, built a 24/7 lifestyle product offering, redesigned our stores worldwide, and renewed our culture and the way we work. I am deeply grateful to everyone who made this possible.”

Grieder continued: “With this strong foundation in place, I am convinced that now is the right time for me to step down and hand over to the next generation of leadership. It has been an honor to lead Hugo Boss, and I will always feel connected to its people and brands.”

Daniel Grieder and Boss ambassador David Beckham.

In May 2026, Hugo Boss sales fell 6% and have declined further since, attributing this to the latest phase in the Claim 5 turnaround strategy, “Claim 5 Touchdown”, which began in December 2025, focusing on brand equity, relevance, and long-term profitability over short-term volume growth. During Q3 earnings, the company shared new guidance for fiscal 2026, forecasting a high-single-digit decline, attributed to weakened demand and ongoing uncertainty.

In June this year, Frasers Group put forward a €2 billion (€38 per share) takeover proposal to Hugo Boss. The German company considered it “financially inadequate”, urging shareholders to reject it. However, Frasers continued to push, progressively upping its stake in the company. In August, Frasers increased its stake to 47.89%, edging closer to majority stakeholder status. Frasers Group CEO Michael Murray assumed the Hugo Boss chair position in September, after Stephan Sturm stepped down.

In October, the British retail conglomerate raised its stake to approximately 50.08% — an additional purchase of 198,666 shares, equating to €7.63 million, according to the stock market filing. The German fashion company became a subsidiary of the Mike Ashley-owned Frasers business. This year, Frasers has continued its aggressive M&A play, buying out Harvey Nichols, acquiring a stake in Under Armour, and upping its stake in Burberry. The Frasers portfolio also includes Flannels, The Webster, Sports Direct, and Slazenger, among others.

“On behalf of the supervisory board, I would like to sincerely thank Daniel for his dedication and his contribution to Hugo Boss,” said Murray in a statement. “Under his leadership, the company sharpened its positioning and renewed the way the brands connect with customers around the world. We respect his decision to step down.”

#6704. I Found the Most Comfortable Pointed-Toe Boots

Every product on this page was chosen by a Harper's BAZAAR editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

Buying pointed-toe boots has always been a challenge for me because I’m built like a ballerina—not, sadly, in terms of long legs or elegant arms or a swanlike neck, but in terms of feet. I have the bunions of a woman who has dedicated her life to the art of dance, which is ironic because I took ballet lessons for all of three months when I was eight. (I quit after they let me wear the tutu, which was really the only thing I was in it for.) I am confessing this not because I enjoy talking about my feet on the internet, but to establish my credibility when I say that I have finally found a pair of slim, sexy, pointed-toe boots that are comfortable enough to wear all day, even for those of us with less-than-ideal extremities.

Margaux’s Inga boots have a long, squared-off toe and a little kitten heel that measures 1.5 inches—tall enough to give you a bit of a lift, but low enough to be walkable. They come in black leather and a sleek espresso suede, both of which look great with jeans but would also be cute peeking out of long, drapey trousers. The best part is the sizing: Margaux offers its boots in narrow, medium, and wide, and somehow, through the magic of proportion play, the wide does not look wide. They accommodate the fullest part of my foot without looking bulky or breaking up the nice long line.

The first time I wore them, it was to a witches’ dinner that my friend Mo throws every Halloween. She invites 30 of her best female friends over, decorates her home in high goth style, and serves us a theatrically witchy meal. (This time, it was black squid-ink pasta.) Of course, one has to dress appropriately to dine with the coven, so I paired the boots with slim black jeans and a sheer black polka-dotted top. Not only did I get a bunch of compliments, but I didn’t find myself pining for my broomstick on the walk home—the boots were just as comfortable at the end of the evening as they’d been at the start of the night.

They’ve held up equally well on the commute to work. In addition to the extra width, they also come with five millimeters of cushioning on the inside, which is enough to protect you when you’re pounding the pavement. Ever since slimmer toes reentered the fashion conversation, I’ve been faced with the choice between sitting out the trend or hobbling around in boots that fundamentally do not fit. As much as I love a good pair of shoes, I also live for a long walk, and the Ingas, miraculously, let me have both. Really, they don’t feel like heels at all, which is a rare and wonderful thing for a pair of pointed-toe kitten-heel boots.

#6703. How This Flexible Balm Foundation Held Up to My 12-Hour Day

The skin care-enhanced formula glides on easily and doesn’t quit.

As a mom in my 40s, I ask a lot of my foundation. I have less time to spend in front of the mirror, yet my skin demands more attention: There are acne scars, hyperpigmentation, and redness to cover, plus dryness that makes it tricky to blend makeup seamlessly. Heavy foundations can easily settle into my fine lines, emphasize my pores, and mute my glow. I need a foundation that’s hydrating yet lightweight, with coverage that’s buildable and easy to touch up during long days.

Unfortunately, not many foundations check all of these boxes. I know this firsthand: I’ve been writing about beauty products for more than 15 years and have tested most of the popular options out there. Few seem designed with mature skin in mind, and most tend to become cakey and dry, especially during midday touch-ups.

But L’Oréal Paris True Match Hyaluron Tinted Balm Foundation fits the bill. It’s made using 80 percent skin care ingredients, including skin-plumping hyaluronic acid. That helps the formula hydrate and smooth skin while also minimizing fine lines and wrinkles over time. Here’s my detailed review of how this foundation looked and felt from morning until night.

I tested the Tinted Balm Foundation ahead of a long, meeting-packed weekday. Using the included teardrop-shaped sponge applicator, I applied and blended from the center of my face outward. The narrow tip let me precisely target the corners of my nose and my dark under-eye circles, and build coverage, so I didn’t need concealer. Then, as I blended the foundation across my cheeks and forehead, it melted right in for that elusive second-skin finish.

One thing I noticed right away: This foundation’s luminous tinted-balm texture is unique, in a good way. It sank into my skin for effortless blending and was so lightweight and breathable that I even felt comfortable using it on my chin, which is prone to hormonal acne thanks to perimenopause. Boosting radiance at a time when my skin has been growing more dry and dull, it also blurred imperfections, including the hard-to-cover redness around my nose and melasma on my forehead.

The foundation comes in a neat mirrored compact, which is much more convenient for on-the-go touch-ups than a messy bottle or tube. After applying it, I tucked it into my crossbody pouch before heading out.

I applied my foundation around 7 A.M. to see how it held up during a 12-hour day of working, exercising, carpooling, and socializing. The verdict: This is one foundation that can actually keep up with a woman over 40—and meet her skin needs.

Mid-morning: The first challenge of the day involved walking my dog around the neighborhood. I live on the coast of Maine, where the weather changes by the hour. The wind and salty mist did a number on my blowout, but my foundation still looked freshly applied and flawless when I checked it prior to a 9:30 A.M. video call for work.

Late morning: My foundation was still going strong at 11 A.M., when I hit the gym. Afterward, I slid the compact out for a quick touch-up, mostly reapplying around my nose and covering a couple of chin pimples. I appreciate that the sponge applicator is antimicrobial, which helps prevent bacteria from exacerbating my acne.

Mid-afternoon: Around 3 P.M., after hours at my laptop, I left to cheer my daughters on in back-to-back high school soccer games. This is the time of day when foundation can start to look tired, especially on mature skin. I snuck out the compact for a quick face check. My foundation had not settled into my crow’s feet, and my skin still looked and felt hydrated and comfortable, not parched. A quick touch-up of my dark circles was all it took to keep my makeup looking on point.

Evening: I arrived home around 8:30 P.M., ate a quick dinner with my family, then did one final complexion inspection before showering. After a long day, including many hours out in the elements and two quick foundation touch-ups, my skin still looked fresh and even.

I’d recommend L’Oréal Paris True Match Hylauron Tinted Balm Foundation to any friends over 40 looking for an easygoing foundation that hydrates, minimizes imperfections, and boosts glow. The skin care-enhanced formula and convenient compact make this a top pick for anyone juggling the busy schedules and skin concerns that come with middle age.

For all-day comfort, what should you look for in a foundation for mature skin?

To nurture mature skin, look for a foundation that incorporates skin care ingredients such as hyaluronic acid, which helps hydrate and plump skin and ensures smooth application. The formula should be lightweight and buildable enough to cover imperfections without feeling heavy or settling into fine lines.

How can you reapply foundation without it looking cakey?

Start by choosing a lightweight foundation that’s hydrating and buildable, such as L’Oréal Paris True Match Hyaluron Tinted Balm Foundation, and apply it in thin layers. Then, for touch-ups, use the teardrop sponge applicator to precisely dab and blend makeup just where needed, like around the nose or directly onto blemishes and hyperpigmentation.

#6702. What’s Really Going On With Blake and Erika From ‘Love Is Blind’? Let’s Investigate

#6701. Haven and Converse Made One of the Coolest Chucks of the Year

As perfect as the Converse Chuck Taylor is, that hasn’t stopped the OG sneaker brand from pushing the sneaker's limits through countless collaborations that remake the classic Chucks in a million different images. While most of those collabs tend to be flashier, there are a few that stand out for their restraint. Or at least, what appears to be restraint at first glance. After a sellout partnership, Canadian outfitters and tastemakers Haven have reunited with Converse for its second team-up, lifting the vaunted Chuck 70 to new heights.

Haven’s disciplined approach to design considers its roots in Vancouver, the topography and climes therein, and incorporates that into its garments. Think waterproof shells, lightweight insulation, gussets for range of motion. “We think about the real world. What do you actually need to wear and what do you need to make you comfortable, and how to make your day a little bit better,” Haven cofounder Arthur Chmielewski says. “It could be just 1 per cent better. But those little details over time, they make your life a little bit better, right?” But it’s not just optimizing in the most sterile sense. Chmielewski also goes to great lengths to consider both comfort and craft in every product, employing details like Japanese denim and Loro Piana cashmere into the brand’s range. So when it comes to tackling an established iconic product, how does Haven do it?

“If you were to think of a farm-to-table kind of approach, it's like using the best ingredients to make the best food. And we're always thinking about that approach as well from a product standpoint,” Chmielewski says. The sneakers are all about subtle details that sum up to a better experience of something that was already pretty great to begin with. A tonal color palette combines different textures of leather, cashmere suede and hairy suede, giving each pair tactile depth that only becomes more pronounced with wear. The Chuck Taylor’s signature rubber toe cap is also replaced with a natural white leather toe cap, a detail that would go undetected more than five feet away. Practically, Haven’s also added an easy-access side-zip made from high-quality custom YKK Excella zippers as well as an additional rubber sole for longevity.

The full magnitude of the sneaker’s design is left for the wearer to experience. Details like reinforced vamps and eyestays, soft leather lining, and an upgraded Ortholite cushioned insole make the shoes more than just pretty to look at.

”The crew at Haven are just so good at translating their signature aesthetic across all products they touch,” says Matt Sleep, Design Lead for Converse Energy. “You see the shoes and instantly you know it fits into their aesthetic ecosystem. You just know it’s Haven without needing to see a logo wildly emblazoned anywhere.”

For a modern label rooted in the classics, the Chuck Taylor is a fitting project. Because, for Chmielewski, it’s all about making things that will last a long time. From the components to the iconic silhouette, you can bet you’ll see a pair of these knocking around for years to come.

As stars and patrons began to take their seats, Stephen Colbert jokingly pulled out Jeff Goldblum’s chair and Martin Short embraced John Krasinski in a corner: vignettes that signaled the lighthearted and lively program to come.

As the lights dimmed, the crowd marveled as a montage showed the momentous filmography of this year’s honoree, Steven Spielberg: Jaws, Indiana Jones, West Side Story, Jurassic Park, Lincoln, and Minority Report, to name a few. The actor recalled the formative and inspiring experience of watching Jaws for the first time, and cracked jokes about the less-than-desirable jobs he took solely to afford tickets to see Spielberg’s movies at the cinema. Cruise thanked the legendary director for “always being generous to [me] in films, but also being generous to [me] at home” as he, quite literally, jumped off the stage and beelined to his friend and longtime collaborator in the audience to share a long hug.

The sentimental speeches continued, with tributes from Martin Scorsese and Emily Blunt, as well as remarks from Christophe Cherix, MoMA’s David Rockefeller Director, and Rajendra Roy, MoMA’s Celeste Bartos Chief Curator of Film. “There are so many wonderful things about Steven,” Blunt said. “He listens in this beautiful way that you wonder if he’s not quite listening, but he’s capturing you.” And of course, Steve Martin and Martin Short also couldn’t let the night pass without indulging in a comedy bit, with the duo taking to the stage to deliver a hilarious introduction. As Spielberg accepted his honors, he praised MoMA’s film program and Chanel for their enduring support of the medium. He also made sure to thank Chanel for his suit, taking a moment to show off the details and the jacket’s impeccable lining. Spielberg concluded by thanking his wife, Kate Capshaw, for teaching him that “there’s more to living than what we do for a living.”

Drew Barrymore, who got her big break in E.T.almost 45 years ago, took her seat for dinner near comedian Marcello Hernandez, who was delighted to take a selfie with Michelle Pfeiffer. And just when one thought the night was winding down, Colbert stepped on stage to announce that Bruce Springsteen would be performing. After a sentimental introduction summarizing his friendship with Spielberg, The Boss launched into “Dancing in the Dark” right as dessert was served.

What: High jewelry collection and new boutique

#6696. Get to Know the Watchmaker Behind John Mayer’s Latest Pick-Up

When looking for the next big thing in the watch world, there are few better places to check than John Mayer’s wrist. The super collector can make his own Audemars Piguet Royal Oaks, skyrocket the value of a previously underappreciated Rolex Daytona, and help establish new indies. This week, Mayer is co-signing a hyper-limited-edition piece from FVF Genève, a watchmaker you should get to know.

FVF Genève is the brainchild of Spanish-born, Geneva-based watchmaker Franc Vila. Mayer is wearing his latest release: FVF2 Time & Day “Happy Monday,” made in partnership with American watch and jewelry retailer Material Good. On his Instagram, Mayer referred to the collaborators as a “Trifecta of Greatness.” There’s more to this piece than its mesmerizing mother-of-pearl, though. The watch’s design celebrates the idea that, if you love what you do, Monday mornings are actually something to look forward to.

The “Happy Monday” is a limited edition of seven pieces, each of which is engraved with a different day of the week on its rotor. The design is a reminder, as the brand says, that “each day is an opportunity to embrace our calling.” It helps, of course, that this message is delivered by a truly beautiful movement with black-polished surfaces, plenty of beveling and polishing, and great typography. Then there’s the rad day-of-the-week indicator on the dial. Situated between 6 and 9 o’clock, it takes the shape of a subtle gold track with a letter for each day of the week in French. To go with the “Happy Monday” theme, “Lundi” (Monday in French) is the only day represented by a standout green letter.

The dial is the showstopping element on this piece. It’s executed in a sparkly deep-blue mother-of-pearl and accented with thick gold-tone printing in the form of an outer minute track, a sub-seconds display between 4 and 5 o’clock, and bisecting lines that create a classically inspired “sector” design. The interplay of the sector when combined with mother-of-pearl is unusual enough, but add in the retrograde day-of-the-week indicator, and you’ve got a truly compelling combo.

The watch’s 39.5mm case is made out of Grade 5 titanium and features a Titalyt treatment—an electrochemical surface treatment that creates a ceramic-like layer and increases durability and hardness. F.P. Journe is a big fan of this treatment, and FVF uses it to great effect here. The finishing gives the Happy Monday a dark, industrial aesthetic that plays off the mother-of-pearl and gold tones on the dial for a distinctive feel. The watch comes on a matching beads-of-rice bracelet with straight endlinks, further adding to the interplay between vintage and modern inspiration. Finally, the crown and date corrector are located on the left side of the case rather than the right, where they typically sit.

Limited to just seven pieces—not including a unique piece that went to Material Good’s Yoni Ben-Yehuda—the $125,000 Happy Monday is the latest independent watch to receive a co-sign from super-collector John Mayer. Despite his role as Audemars Piguet's “Creative Conduit," Mayer has been known to support high-end independent makers such as F.P. Journe, and famously helped propel Vanguart onto the horological stage over the past year.

Vila, who established his eponymous luxury watch brand in the early 2000s, is a prime candidate to receive his flowers from the modern collecting community: marrying avant-garde case and dial designs with high complications. Vila sold his initial brand in the late 2000s, but he’s now having another go at creating modern classics with FVF. He’s come at the right time. It’s boom times for independent watchmakers as collectors try to identify the next big thing, and a co-sign from Mayer makes FVF a strong candidate to catch fire.

#6695. Léa Seydoux Isn’t Trying to Act. She’s Trying to Live

The French actress continues her string of emotionally demanding roles in The Unknown and Gentle Monster

Léa Seydoux first stepped into the limelight in Christophe Honoré’s The Beautiful Person, where her role as Junie de Chartres earned her the Trophée Chopard award for rising actors at Cannes. From there, she moved seamlessly between highbrow French cinema and Hollywood, achieving a critical breakthrough with Blue Is the Warmest Color in 2013 and starring alongside Daniel Craig as a Bond girl in Spectre and No Time to Die. Most years, she’s starred in at least two films, and 2026 is no exception: She plays a woman with a man’s soul trapped in her body in Arthur Harari’s psychological fantasy The Unknown, and in Marie Kreutzer’s Gentle Monster, releasing on Netflix on November 18, she’s a pianist who unearths her husband’s hideous crimes. The words thorny and barbed read like understatements for both films, and it’s exactly what interests Seydoux about the stories. Like in life itself, she avoids easy answers, opting instead for exploration.

Seydoux got the chance to explore an especially ambitious idea in The Unknown. It tells the story of David Zimmerman (Niels Schneider), a photographer who wakes up in the body of a woman he sleeps with. Seydoux plays both that woman, Eva, and the man trapped within her body. “I felt the movie was something new to me, to play an impossible idea and make it believable, try to give it a truthful dimension,” Seydoux says. She’s no stranger to high-concept stories, previously starring in Bertrand Bonello’s The Beast and David Cronenberg’s Crimes of the Future. Each time, she imbues these characters with humanity, despite their far-fetched sci-fi dilemmas.

“I like movies that make you think, movies that bring up questions, when there’s a debate around the film,” she says. “What I love the most is to explore human nature, our human condition. This is what cinema allows us to do.”

Seydoux might vehemently love movies, yet acting remains a demanding process for her. She relies on the art form to dig into feelings and emotions. “I don’t feel necessarily very comfortable with acting. It’s not a place where I’m like, ‘I love it,’ but at the same time, I find it a bit painful. It’s more a way to experience things and ideas,” she says.

Gentle Monster provides another knotty premise, this time grounded in reality. It follows Lucy Weiss, a famed experimental pianist who gives up her career to raise her young son with her doting husband, Philip (Laurence Rupp). One day, the police knock on their door, and it’s revealed that Philip is accused of distributing child pornography.

“The subject matter is tough, but the fact that it’s through the woman’s perspective—and not through the victim or perpetrator—it’s through her emotions that the story unfolds [is what interested me],” she says. “Things are not too defined, but it’s also because of the subject matter; it was the only way to talk about it. [Marie] gave me a lot of freedom.”

Born in Paris in 1985, Seydoux spent her childhood wedged among seven siblings and half-siblings. She remembers feeling isolated, practically invisible, as a child. “I was always in the shadows in a way,” she says. “As a kid, I felt transparent. I was never at the center of [my] big family.” This plays a big part in her surprise at her acting career, never thinking of herself as someone deserving of center stage, of fame, of attention. In fact, acting never even crossed her mind until she befriended some actors when she turned 18. “I loved the way they lived their lives,” she says. “I admired their life—the fact that they were free.”

And yet, she rejects the label of “actress.” “I try to be truthful as much as possible,” she says. “I try not to act. This is what I try to be, and I’m more into reaction than action.” She adds, “It’s more reactive than acting.”

For Seydoux, “reacting” and really experiencing life is only possible if she “abandons” herself to her characters. One of the most intense examples of this is Abdellatif Kechiche’s controversial lesbian love story Blue Is the Warmest Color, in which she stars alongside Adèle Exarchopoulos. The film’s schedule stretched from two months to five months, and it has since become notorious for its grueling pace. (The famous sex scene took 10 days alone.) “The greatest and most intense experience I’ve had was with Adèle when we did Blue Is the Warmest Color,” she recalls. “It was crazy, and really the connection between us had to be very, very intense. I think, with Adèle, it’s something that will always be a part of me now. There was an exchange, and it was more than making a film. It was really a life experience.”

One scene from Gentle Monster lingered with me for weeks after I watched it: Lucy’s snotty, tearful confrontation with her husband at their family home as she pleads with him to tell the truth. This close-up of Seydoux not only accentuates her famous blue eyes but also shows her uncanny control of this character’s emotions. It feels, for lack of better words, real. Seydoux partly credits her empathy to being a mother of two children, but this scene goes beyond compassion; it shows how much of herself she gives to the character. Before filming this scene, Kreutzer offered little direction, letting her tap into how the character felt. “I prepare myself, and I have to just let myself go and be in the moment and just open up,” Seydoux says, suggesting that perhaps these emotions otherwise lie dormant within her.

I found this is what Seydoux means by “reaction.” Every role in her varied and extolled filmography functions as an avenue through which she can explore what it means to be human, what it means to feel. Her natural curiosity about the world and its inhabitants existed before she decided to act in her teens and will exist long into the future, even if acting jobs don’t remain on the table. “If it ended tomorrow, I’d be happy,” she says. “I will find a way. Now, I really feel that I’m acting because I still have the opportunity. But I have more things to explore, and I would love to have more experiences.”

#6694. Rihanna’s Son Riot Made His Magazine Cover Debut—and She Shared All 6 Versions

Rihanna and A$AP Rocky’s three children are now all magazine cover stars. After their oldest, RZA, made his British Vogue cover debut in 2023 and youngest, Rocki, appeared on two covers this year, middle child Riot Rose is having his turn. The 3-year-old covered Arena Homme+ all on his own, though Rihanna joined him for one shot, wearing the red Loewe jumpsuit she had on when she revealed her pregnancy with him at the 2023 Super Bowl. There are six different versions of his cover, and his proud mother shared every image.

Last month, Rocky hinted at Riot’s cover in an interview with The Cut. He told the outlet, “One of my sons has a modeling gig in like three days, you know, the day before my birthday, and it’s—I’m so proud of him; this is his first magazine cover, so I think it’s just fascinating to see these little people grow into personalities of their own. It’s trippy, just in retrospect, thinking back when they were just so small and little. I mean, they’re still relatively little and small, but you know, they kind of speak up for themselves and have their own kind of swag and shit. It’s crazy.”

While RZA and Rocki posed with their parents, Riot’s cover was all about him. Rihanna teased he was a lot like her in her 2025 interview with Harper’s Bazaar.

“Riot, he’s just hilarious,” she said. “When he wakes up, he starts to squeal, scream. Not in a crying way. He just wants to sing. And I’m like, ‘Okay, here we go!’ He’s my alarm in the morning! He’s not taking no for an answer from anyone. I don’t know where he came from, dude.”

She added that Riot’s big brother, RZA, at first struggled with losing his only-child status “like all [new] siblings do, and at first Riot was understanding that his role was being the little brother. Now he knows he’s in charge.”

Last night, supermodel Christy Turlington stepped out at the Museum of Modern Art’s 2026 Annual Film Benefit in New York, wearing a knit dress from Matthieu Blazy’s fall 2026 Chanel collection. A dress this graphic and eye-catching needs makeup to balance it, and Turlington paired it with black eyeliner and a glossy ruby-red lipstick.

While we don’t know the exact shade she wore last night, it’s clearly a formula that sits somewhere between a satin lipstick and a gloss-balm, with pigment that doesn’t sacrifice moisture or shine. Turlington is a Lancôme ambassador, so it could be the brand’s Lip Idole Butterglow Hydrating Lip Balm or L’Absolu Rouge Cream Lipstick. Otherwise, Chanel makes a gorgeous option in both the Rouge Coco Flash and Rouge Allure Extrait formulas. These formulas subtly plump and moisturize dry lips while blurring lip lines and imperfections.

Lancôme L'Absolu Rouge Moisturizing Cream Lipstick in 397 Berry Noir

Chanel Hydrating Vibrant Shine Lip Colour

Lancome Lip Idole Squalane-12 Butterglow Hydrating Lip Balm

The best part of this look is that it proves you don’t need to match your lipstick exactly to your outfit, as long as they’re in the same color family. While the Chanel dress is more of an orange-red knit, Turlington’s lipstick is a more neutral ruby that harmonizes with the warm tones and shades in the rest of her look. Plus, raspberry or ruby-red lipstick can brighten your face in seconds, even with little to no other makeup.

Bold lipstick is a bit outside Turlington’s day-to-day comfort zone; she told Bazaar recently that she’s “definitely an old-school Carmex or ChapStick kind of person, because I’m constantly reapplying it to my dry lips, especially in the winter.” The rest of her routine is equally as effortless: “I wash my face in the morning and moisturize a lot. Sometimes I even double-moisturize because, especially at this time of year, I get dry skin. And then, I’ll add a nice little layer of foundation, some blush, and mascara, and that’s kind of it, I’m on my way.”

#6688. Dua Lipa Has Already Got Her Hands on Winter’s Next It Coat

There is a certain kind of winter coat that’s popular right now. Dua Lipa, a longtime devotee of the fabulous, fantastical coat, understands this better than most. It’s one that requires very little else of its wearer. No elaborate styling or carefully coordinated separates needed. Just throw it on over a pair of jeans, and you're dressed. The coat is the outfit!

And so the singer has offered a first look at a yet-to-be-released piece from London-based designer Charlotte Simone’s forthcoming Winter Drop 2. The jacket features an enormous, shaggy brown collar, extravagant furry cuffs, and a cropped silhouette. Lipa wore hers with faded blue Icon Denim Didy jeans and a black Bottega Veneta Madison shoulder bag, allowing the outerwear to take center stage.

“Dua is a dream girl,” Simone tells Vogue. "She never looks overdone or precious about what she’s wearing. She’ll throw one of our coats over a simple pair of jeans or a slip dress, and suddenly the coat is the whole look. That’s exactly how I design… I want every style to be the statement, the piece that makes you feel instantly put together the moment you step out the door.”

Certainly, the fantasy coat is having quite the moment. Jennifer Lawrence has been wandering around New York in a sumptuous chartreuse velvet robe by Colleen Allen; Carelli’s vintage-inflected, fur-trimmed coats have been dominating London streets; and Kendall Jenner and Hailey Bieber have both fallen for Conner Ives’s extraordinary embroidered silk robes with lavish furry collars and cuffs. Forget sensible or anonymous winter layers: This season, outerwear is an opportunity for a little theater, with unexpected colors or an excess of fluff.

But Charlotte Simone was doing the statement coat long before this latest wave of maximalist winter dressing. Founded by Charlotte Simone Beecham, the London-based label has spent the better part of a decade cultivating a devoted following for its nostalgic Penny Lane jackets, exaggerated faux-fur collars and cuffs, fuzzy textures, and playful proportions. Taylor Swift, Gigi Hadid, Charli XCX, and Lila Moss are among the famous fans who have fallen under its spell. So distinctive are the designs that they have become instantly recognizable on the street.

Lipa herself is something of a repeat customer. Just a few weeks ago, she stepped out in New York wearing the brand's inky blue-black, wonderfully fuzzy Lila jacket, styled with light-wash denim, chunky black Chrome Hearts boots, oversized sunglasses, and a Chanel bag. The formula was much the same, an otherwise straightforward outfit transformed by one gloriously tactile piece of outerwear.

Part of Charlotte Simone’s enduring appeal is its deliberate approach to production. Rather than churning out endless collections, the label operates through a handful of carefully considered, limited-edition drops each year. Designed in London and produced in small batches with an emphasis on quality and longevity, its most coveted styles routinely sell out within minutes. The first winter drop, released in October, was especially personal: conceived by Simone during early mornings nursing her newborn, it drew on the golden hues of dawn, the romance of winter mornings, and the optimism of new beginnings.

Now comes Drop 2, and Lipa has already provided a persuasive preview. “I love her confidence,” Simone says. “She doesn’t chase trends; she wears what she loves and makes it entirely her own, and that’s the spirit of Charlotte Simone.”

In an era of increasingly extravagant outerwear, Dua Lipa knows that the Charlotte Simone coat doesn’t demand that you dress up. It does the dressing up for you. Set your alarms for Drop 2!

#6686. Here’s Every Track Lisa Performed on Night 1 of Her Viva La Lisa Residency

Lisa has finally touched down for the first date of her Viva La Lisa residency in Las Vegas. On November 12, the Blackpink rapper made history as the first K-pop act to perform a Las Vegas residency date at The Colosseum at Caesars Palace, and to celebrate the occasion, she hit the stage with several hits from her catalog.

Lisa opened up the show with her recently released single, “Tarantino,” and continued the rest of her 90-minute set with tracks from both of her eras, including her new six-track EP, Press Play. “Cobra,” “Sweat,” “V12,” “Cobra,” and “Cut U Off” were highlighted throughout the setlist, with “SaWaDiKa” closing the evening.

The rapper’s solo album Alter Ego also received its fair share of time throughout the setlist’s five chapters. “Badgrrrl” and “Fxck Up the World” were the first from the album to appear during the show, but deeper into the concert, fan-favorite tracks like “Rockstar,” “New Woman,” “Moonlit Floor,” and “Dream” also appeared in the program.

Longtime fans of Lisa were also treated to hits from the earliest days of her solo career. “Money,” her second independent single released in 2021, had its time to shine during the second chapter of her concert, though fans missed out on hearing her first solo track, “Lalisa,” on the setlist.

Lisa’s Viva La Lisa residency was announced as a four-show engagement but was upgraded to include five more dates due to overwhelming fan demand after the first set of dates sold out in 10 minutes. The remaining dates of the residency will take place on November 13, 14, and 27-29.

#6685. Elias Matso Is the Twisted Corsetier Dressing Sydney Sweeney and Jenna Ortega

The young designer talked to Bazaar about craftsmanship, fittings, and developing his signature technique

These days, Elias Matso is known for twisted corsetry worn by the likes of Sydney Sweeney and Jenna Ortega. But the first time he noticed the impact of a good costume, he was a kid watching Julie Andrews in Victor/Victoria. He sat by the TV watching the Oscar-winning actor perform “Le Jazz Hot!” in Art Deco gowns, decadent headpieces, and dramatic feathered capes. “I know she was acting in that scene, but I just felt like she was so happy to be wearing those costumes,” he tells Harper’s Bazaar. “And I was obsessed with that.”

Matso is now 24, and it’s easy to see the impact of that moment on his creative approach. A recent graduate of Polimoda in Florence with Charles James, Bob Mackie, Mugler, and Mr. Pearl on his mood board, he crafts avant-garde, couture corsetry. (It’s perhaps no surprise that he has a history of making costumes for drag performers.) His approach is personal and intimate, rooted in hand craftsmanship and collaborative dialogue with clients.

In October 2025, Sweeney made waves when she wore a crystal naked dress, pulled from Christian Cowan’s Spring/Summer 2026 collection and made in collaboration with the young designer. The piece featured twisted corsetry and a semi-sheer body that hugged the Euphoria star’s body—and, naturally, the public had quite a lot to say about it. “I did not anticipate that it would be as big as it was,” the artist admits. “It was really cool that the conversation left fashion and became a bigger conversation about women’s bodies and what modesty should look like or shouldn’t look like. And how a lot of the world doesn’t know what boobs look like.”

While the discourse surprised Matso, it reflected one of his own core beliefs: that “fashion is at least 50% the person who’s wearing the thing.” He keeps this in mind during fittings, ensuring clients feel comfortable and beautiful every step of the way. Below, he talks to Bazaar about his early references, his focus on craftsmanship, and the colorful steel-boning dress recently worn by Jenna Ortega.

As a kid, I had a paper doll of myself, and whenever there were clothes that I wanted that I didn’t have, I would make them for the paper doll. It was pocket sized, and whenever I was bored—which was all the time, because I have attention deficit issues—I would pull it out and play.

It is. It was my third year and I wanted to explore the tension that children hold, when they feel like they’re growing faster than they can keep up with, and feeling at odds with themselves, because that’s how I felt when I was a kid. There was this feeling, especially in the queer world, of being pulled in different directions, gender-wise. And so I had developed that idea, and then through sketching and conversations with my teachers, we started getting more and more towards this very literal idea of a twist. And then the collaboration that I did with Christian Cowan pushed it further.

I was in New York over the summer before my senior year, and I was looking for jobs and not getting anything. I started looking into scooping ice cream at Van Leeuwen’s and stuff like that. And then, one day, I got a text from Alicia Keys’s stylist and a DM from Christian that was like, “Do you want to do some dresses for my show?” It was a good day.

It actually wasn’t originally supposed to be that fabric. We couldn’t find the fabric we wanted, and we couldn’t figure out how to put as many stones as we needed onto the fabric that we found. Then we just found this sheer fabric, and we were like, “Okay, it’s going to be the original dress, but it’s going to be completely see-through.”

I made it to fit this gorgeous six-foot-tall model from Finland. And this is why fit is so fun, because with that dress, there was this miracle where it fit her so perfectly one way, and then it fit Sydney, who has completely different proportions, in this totally other, also beautiful way. Often when things get pulled from a runway, they don’t fit like that. And it was just really cool to see.

I really like meeting people in person when I can because it just always creates a better outcome. I feel like the conversation is so much about your personality, but also your physiology, the way you’re built and the way you’re made up. People’s bodies respond differently. So it’s really important to do fittings and to check in with people before, during, and after the fitting, and ask, “How intense of an experience do you want this to be? What will make you feel the most beautiful, the most comfortable?”

Sometimes a little bit of discomfort is part of being comfortable, but you have to have signed up for that. That’s my thing that I’ve learned: Discomfort, if you’re prepared, can be part of it. But there has to be a conversation if discomfort is involved, or else we are forgetting that fashion is at least 50% the person who’s wearing the thing.

When I start a collection, I’m always looking through the archives of a museum, like the Whitney or often the Guggenheim, because you have less control over what you’re going to find. [For this piece,] I had found one painting that led me to Mark Ranger’s website. And we got in touch and then collaborated the whole year. It turns out we explore a lot of the same themes. Here, the dress was supposed to be about time and our body’s relationship to gravity and this idea of melting, not in a way that we’re trying to resist and slow down, but in a way that’s just natural and beautiful.

The goal was to make something unrecognizable, but using recognizable techniques. I already had a lot of steel boning because it’s the same stuff that’s inside all these corsets. And so I just got more, and then I started chopping it up into smaller and smaller pieces. I was able to create a relationship with Preciosa, who does crystals for a lot of big brands—I met them through a trip that they did to my school. I just came up with this weird technique that was, I guess, a test of my own physical and mental strength in a way.

I didn’t make it with Jenna in mind. I never thought it would have all these different lives and stages.

I guess I’m seeing it less and less valued in fashion. And even when something is hand-done and comes out gorgeous and successful, the people that wind up getting the praise for those things are not the people who do the thing, but the people who have curated those artisans—the artistic directors, the designers. My friends and I have just graduated, we’re looking for work, and I see my friends who have really singular skills getting so undervalued for their work and their time. That is something that is really frustrating to me. And in an age where so many things can be falsified via technology and the internet, I think things that you can’t fake are how something’s made, how something stands up over time, how something feels on the inside when you put it on. And designers care less and less about that, I guess.

I’m in a transitional stage where I’m not sure what I’m gonna do next. Every day, I get people asking me to make dresses on this scale for free or for bafflingly low amounts of money. You know, I’m told all the time that there’s no budget for things. People want couture for no budget. People in this industry have no shame when it comes to asking for that. For emerging designers, there are so many of us that they know that if I can’t supply what they’re looking for, they will find another independent designer who has the resources or the funds or the ability to provide that thing for less than what it’s worth. I do worry about that. But this press is making me think that maybe there is a niche for something that walks the line between art and fashion and not in the aesthetic sense, which people talk about all the time, but in the financial and logistical sense. So that’s what I’m trying to figure out.

Also, I found that if people are asking for things for free, it’s very rarely the client themselves. It’s often their team. I love the art of styling, but that is another reason that I find one-on-one relationships and conversations with the person who you’re going to be dressing really important. It makes them understand the level of attention or care that they are interacting with.

This is still in process, but I’m working on a piece with Laverne Cox. I always wanted to work with her. And then starting to work with her, I was like, “I was right.” Because she has such appreciation and respect for the process of everything and the details and how everything works. She’s a really respectful and engaging patron, and we’ve had a lot of interesting conversations about the designers that we both look up to.

For me, I want to take the momentum that I have and do something that feels exciting with it. And at the same time, I am not sure that I have the experience to start a company, you know? I am in conversations with lots of people who I’ve always wanted to collaborate with, and it’s so exciting. Really, really exciting and mind-blowing. And at the same time, I’m reaching out to brands that I admire to see what openings they have because we all need stability. I’m trying to remain as flexible as possible.

#6684. Sneak Inside GQ’s Breakouts House Party Deep in the Hollywood Hills

GQ’s Breakouts have officially broken containment. Last night, high up in the Hollywood hills, at one of LA’s most famous spots—the glass-and-concrete modernist sculpture known as the Sheats-Goldstein residence—GQ toasted to a new class of stars who spent 2026 commanding our attention.

First, they had to get in, which was no small feat. Guests were Ubered to the residence, then transferred to golf carts which took them down a palm-lined path, past the apple-red twin-engined car brought by presenting sponsor Hot Wheels, across the mildly perilous path over a koi pond—to a tucked-away den where GQ Editor-in-chief Adam Baidawi quickly toasted the 13 Breakouts of 2026. “The double edged sword of success is that sometimes you’re so out-of-your mind busy and stressed and locked in, that you forget to enjoy it,” he told the room. “I hope you find a moment to enjoy it tonight.” And then he laid out the evening’s goals: have a hell of a house party. Everyone obliged.

GQ Breakouts Stavros Halkias and Pablo Torre huddled with Hasan Piker, who later chatted with Jake Shane, creating a powerful personality vortex. Amelia Dimoldenberg sipped an espresso martini at the bar in the house’s club. Breakout Belmont Cameli hung out poolside on the terrace, soaking up cinematic views of a glittering LA, while DJ Alice Longyu Gao played classic bangers like Drake and Future’s “Diamonds Dancing” filled the air. Later, towards the end of the night, two guests went rogue and got themselves escorted out for diving into the pool in their underwear. (In a shocking twist, it was not Stav, who had shouted “Cannonball!” earlier, by the house’s other pool.) Houseparty’s gonna houseparty.

When I found GQ Breakout Pablo Torre outside, he was showing off the incredible business card that house owner Jimmy Goldstein had given him just moments before. It was huge, about the size of an index card you used to study for algebra tests. Rare memorabilia.

Torre—who made the NBA’s life difficult with reporting that blew open the Kawhi Leonard scandal—joked to me that Clippers fandom is so tepid in LA that he hardly felt like he had to watch his back while in town from New York. (The biggest concern for his visit: a rainy forecast for the weekend.)

As Breakout AZ Chike told GQ for his portfolio interview, people “crossed worlds that hadn’t been crossed before.” Chike parlayed fellow Breakout Cameli early in the night before taking the stage a few hours later to run through heaters like “Packed Up” and “Look Like My Mama”—the same tracks that earned him GQ Breakout status. He told me he’s enjoying being back home in LA after touring his new album across the country, playing in new-for-him cities. Turns out DC showed an unexpected amount of love to a West Coast kid.

GQ Breakout Owen Thiele celebrated the season 3 renewal of Adults—announced earlier in the day—by zipping around the party armed with a disposable film camera. Watching him connect with True Whitaker of I Love LA felt like witnessing the cinematic crossover that we lowkey need to see play out on-screen.

Mavi, the North Carolina rapper who popped up in GQ’s September best new music portfolio, told me he’s finishing the project that he teased back then. He says he has so many songs in the tuck that he might thank his fans by dropping more than we’d expect.

Speaking of fresh music from new talents, Leon Thomas said he isn’t tripping expectations for his follow-up to the critically acclaimed, Grammy-winning “Mutt,” and previewed a project that’ll source inspiration from “p-funk, soul, and hip-hop.” Thomas was in the midst of rehearsing for an appearance at Tyler, The Creator’s Flog Gnaw festival this weekend, and joked that he got so sweaty during practice that we can expect him to tear it down on Saturday.

For the moment though, the weather was perfect, the music was hitting, the vibes were strong, and there was a lot more night left for partying. See how it all went down below. ✦

#6681. ‘We Just Are So Gagged’: Jordan Firstman and Reggie Absolom on Club Kid’s Success

The film’s stars discuss their excitement, their music tastes, and how they interpret that ending.

This story contains spoilers for Club Kid.

For his debut feature film, Club Kid, Jordan Firstman envisioned a curly-haired boy who could live in a world of adults. The story was well established by the time casting agent Carmen Cuba met British actor Reggie Absolom, who had appeared in Silo and other series. Firstman, who wrote, directed, and starred in the film, knew he was the perfect one to play Arlo, the 10-year-old son that Firstman’s character Peter never knew he had. Firstman and Absolom grew close quickly and developed a unique friendship that hasn’t slowed down post-filming. “We text all day,” Firstman says.

The pair spoke to ELLE about Reggie getting to DJ for the film, whether he’ll have a Radiohead phase, and what the movie says about family.

Jordan Firstman: I had a very extensive list of things I wanted in the character, and my casting director was like, “You really need to manage your expectations because you’re looking for a child actor. Baseline, you have to find someone good.” I also just wanted them to be naturally cool and not feel like a child actor [but] feel like a kid. I wanted them to have curly hair. I wanted them to look enough like me that they could be my kid. In the script, the character is written as half Indian, and she was like, “Babe, you’re just not going to find all of that.”

I found Reggie, and he checked every box. He looked like the kid I had in my head when I wrote it. He also was a really natural actor and nothing felt forced. I sent him a playlist of songs I wrote the movie to, and he told me which ones he liked. I thought he had really good taste, and we just talked for a while and got ice cream. And then it wasn’t until in the process that I found out he was a quarter Indian too. He literally had every single thing that I wanted, and so it did feel like a miracle in a lot of ways.

Reggie Absolom: It was a bit weird at first. But then I became such good friends with everyone anyway and it just felt like I fit in there. It didn’t matter how old I was. I was just friends with everyone, and I was just working like they were as well.

JF: I love sending people that I love music. Reggie’s music taste influenced the characters. He was into Slipknot at the time, so I wrote a little Slipknot into the script, and he also liked Massive Attack and Cocteau Twins, once I sent him my playlist. I wrote that in.

There’s this whole other component of the actual club music, on which we collaborated so closely with David Peck, who’s in the movie [and who wrote songs for the film and performed them as Heather Asylum]. He did Reggie’s whole DJ set and River Moon consulted. We had real DJs in the scene helping me and making sure we had all the right tracks. The music in the movie is everything; it’s the throughline in the story and the construction of the movie.

RA: You get most of the credit. You gave me quite a few songs, like Cocteau Twins ones and really good Massive Attack ones. I was like, okay, I’m going to go deeper into these and listen to all of their albums. Now there’s some songs that I would’ve never really listened to. When I listened to Cocteau Twins, I would’ve been like, “Okay, this is weird.” But now I’m like, “Okay, maybe I like the weird kind of songs.”

JF: I think you’re going to also have a major Radiohead era.

RA: Maybe, but I don’t know. I don’t like Radiohead.

JF: We were going to do “Maybe I’m Amazed” by Paul McCartney, and he wasn’t responding to our emails about licensing it. The day before [we filmed the scene], I was trying to think of other songs, and “Thoroughfare” is my favorite song, I think ever. I feel like I would be that dad that made my kid play Ethel Cain on the piano with me. Then we played it, and it felt really cute and really sincere. We still sang Paul McCartney, but they were like, “You don’t need Paul McCartney. Don’t waste your money.” And “Thoroughfare” is the vibe.

RA: It got me into a lot of different types of music, which I’m happy about. DJing was really fun and something that I’d want to do in the future. Maybe not a full-time job, but something on the side to do, something fun.

RA: It didn’t really influence the roles I wanted to get, but now that I’m in a film that’s done so well, it’s opened up for me to maybe get bigger roles than I would’ve expected before filming this.

RA: The idea of being in a movie, that was the next step for me. I was filming maybe three episodes of a series. I felt like no matter the role, just being in the movie would be the next thing to do. Then the fact that this was a lead role and that I felt similar to Arlo personality-wise in some ways. I felt like I could perform really naturally with the things that Arlo says and the way that he acts.

JF: Kramer vs. Kramer is such a classic and a movie I love. I often reference An Unmarried Woman with Jill Clayburgh. I love her relationship with her daughter in that movie and how they treat each other like adults. Because Peter has no experience with kids, he doesn’t know how to treat them like anything else but how he treats everyone.

JF: Once I started writing it, I started really understanding Peter and Arlo and what they needed. I actually feel like it’s a gift that they didn’t end up together for both of their lives for that time. That phone call [at the end] is so important, because the door opens again once they’re ready. I think it would’ve been too intense for Peter to [raise Arlo full-time]....He still wasn’t completely out of the party scene. He was still selling drugs. He was not ready to really do this in a real way. Arlo really needed a year of knowing true stability and a normal childhood.

But I think what Peter and his community offered Arlo was a very different version of normal. They encouraged creativity. For a traumatized kid, having an art practice is everything. In my darkest times as a kid, I turned to art. To me, it’s a very human ending, and to me it’s hopeful.

RA: Both of them needed to have that break. They’re trying to find themselves and what they should do. Now, another thing, whilst Arlo was with Peter, he was getting no education really. He tried to get him into school.

RA: He just gave up on that. The ending also leaves it up to interpretation what happens to them in the future. Obviously, it could have been like, oh, they rejoin and they’re father and son forever. I think it’s nicer when the film has an ending that’s up to interpretation a bit, where there could be different branches on the ending.

JF: He really enjoyed fatherhood, so I think he will continue his relationship with Arlo and help him through his teen years and grow up.

RA: In my opinion, Peter with a baby, adopting a baby would be a bit, like Edison says, “He’s all prepared. Forget the trauma,” or something like that.

RA: He could do it. He’d need Oscar [Peter’s partner, played by Diego Calva].

JF: No one involved in this project has had this happen to them. Even Cara [Delevingne] has never been a part of something like this. We just are so gagged. We can’t believe this is happening and that people are responding to it in this way. We get standing ovations everywhere we go, and it’s surreal. We don’t take for granted that this is a rare thing that happens.

This interview has been edited and condensed for clarity.

#6678. Anna Sui on the Five Films That Inspired Her Aesthetic

Here at Bazaar, we are just as devoted to the well-dressed mind as we are to the well-dressed woman. In fact, we find that one often engenders the other. In our new series The Well-Dressed Mind, we examine the intersection point between style and intellect by asking industry professionals and tastemakers for their cultural recommendations.

Anna Sui’s namesake brand is rooted in a reverence for the past. By blending niche references across time periods, she makes her clothes feel distinctly now. Part of a defining generation of downtown New York designers in the ’80s and ’90s, Sui invokes her love of vintage fashion, design, photography, and art as the basis of her work. The feel of the resulting collections is at once girlish, grunge, ’70s, punk, and bohemian.

Last week, the Friends of the Costume Institute, an organization attached to the Met museum, asked Sui to dive into her vast collection of archival references and select a film that most influenced her as a designer for a screening. (Sui also funds a yearlong internship for the department.) She picked the 1970 movie Performance, directed by Donald Cammell and Nicolas Roeg, which depicts a London gangster’s identity crisis while in hiding at the home of a rock star (played by Mick Jagger) and his two girlfriends, one of whom is played by style icon Anita Pallenberg. You can see why this would appeal to her; the trippy, ’70s clash of glam and bohemia is very Sui.

Hungry for more, we asked Sui to outline the onus behind that selection and four additional films that had the greatest influence on her aesthetic.

Directed by Donald Cammell and Nicolas Roeg

“Anita Pallenberg has always been my style icon, especially since I saw her amazing wardrobe throughout Performance: the fringe kaftan, antique lace top, pink velvet pants, fox fur coat, silver platform sandals, texture zigzag tights, and the slinky black satin dresses.”

“This film is set in a brothel in 1930s fascist Italy. The lingerie, piano shawls with smoky eye makeup and wavy bobs looked straight out of a Sarah Moon photograph.”

“Jane Birkin is a fashion model with a Peeping Tom for a neighbor. He’s obsessed with what he perceives as her glamorous fashion lifestyle, and he comes to the rescue when she decides to do herself in. It’s got sets by the artistic collective the Fool, which designed the Beatles’ Apple Boutique, and a George Harrison soundtrack to transport you to the swinging ’60s in London.”

“The Who’s rock opera has a star-studded cast: Ann-Margret, Oliver Reed, Jack Nicholson, Elton John, Eric Clapton, Keith Moon, Tina Turner, and Roger Daltrey. There are amazing costumes by his wife, Shirley Russell, including Biba clothes on their daughter Victoria. This musical odyssey is filled with the amazing Who soundtrack.”

“Liza Minnelli's talent and effervescent personality brought to life the dynamo Sally Bowles. With an incredible cast—divinely decadent Joel Grey, gorgeous Michael York, and Marisa Berenson—we're transported to the Kit Kat Club and 1930s Weimar Republic Germany. The songs and music are just as sensational as Bob Fosse’s choreography and direction. And Liza’s costumes, with a helping hand from Halston, are legendary. She even wears an embellished Ossie Clark for one musical number. Her green nail polish, spiky false eyelashes, and signature haircut have stayed with me forever. One of the greatest musical dramas of all time.”

#6677. FKA Twigs’s Josephine Baker Transformation Is Already a Beauty Spectacle

With lacquered curls spiraling across her forehead, a dark and smoky gaze, and a megawatt smile, FKA twigs has all but disappeared into Josephine Baker. The first image of the British musician as the legendary entertainer in the forthcoming biopic Josephine Baker has arrived, and if this is anything to go by, we’re in for an on-screen beauty transformation for the ages.

In the image, twigs stands atop a dining table, twisting into a playful pose in a pink, crystal-strewn flapper dress with delicate beading and fringe. But it’s the beauty that really transports us to 1920s Paris. Her hair has been molded into an ultra-glossy, close-cropped style, with elaborate kiss curls arranged across her forehead and temples. Her eyes are rimmed with smoldering shadow, her brows sharply defined, and her lips painted a rich red. It’s classic Baker, down to the mischievous expression.

After all, few performers have left such an enduring mark on beauty history. Baker’s signature Eton crop, sculpted finger waves, and intricate S-shaped kiss curls helped define the Jazz Age. She understood the transformative potential of hair and makeup: brows drawn into fine, expressive arches, heavily kohled eyes, and dark, precisely shaped lips. Hers was a highly theatrical, unapologetically glamorous approach to beauty, one that challenged conventional standards and continues to inform red-carpet trends a century later.

You need only look at the recent Met Galas for proof. At the 2025 event, Baker’s influence was everywhere: Dua Lipa, Sydney Sweeney, and Coco Jones were among those sporting intricate forehead curls, while Gigi Hadid and twigs herself paid tribute to the entertainer through their clothing. The following year, the kiss curl remained a red-carpet fixture, appearing in elaborate interpretations on Lisa and Kylie Jenner. Elsewhere, Ayo Edebiri, Odessa A’zion, and Chappell Roan have all experimented with variations of the look in 2026.

A fellow dancer, singer, and consummate performer, twigs has long treated beauty as an extension of her artistic expression, experimenting with sculptural hairstyles and otherworldly makeup. Baker was celebrated for an exuberant, often comedic stage persona, finding ways to subvert the expectations and racial stereotypes imposed upon her. Their aesthetics aren’t identical—twigs gravitates toward the experimental and occasionally surreal, where Baker delighted in humor and Jazz Age showmanship—but both understand the power of a carefully constructed image.

Indeed, twigs has already explored Baker’s beauty codes. At the 2025 Met Gala, she wore an ultra-short Eton crop and a Josephine-inspired feathered dress by Grace Wales Bonner. Speaking to Vogue at the time, she described Baker, alongside Eartha Kitt and Grace Jones, as an embodiment of female dandyism. The admiration clearly runs deep.

The forthcoming film, directed by Maïmouna Doucouré, will follow Baker’s extraordinary life from her ascent to stardom in 1920s Paris through her work with the French Resistance during World War II and her involvement in the American civil rights movement. Aunjanue Ellis-Taylor stars as Baker’s mother, with the production spanning multiple decades and locations. Filming reportedly began this fall.

The project marks the first major screen adaptation of the Baker’s life and has received the full blessing of the late singer’s estate. “She lives on in our hearts as a visionary, ground-breaking woman whose story is as powerful as it is relevant today,” twigs said in a press statement.

The expansive timeline offers a sweeping beauty playground for lead makeup artist Laura Ozier, working alongside costume designer Emmanuelle Youchnovski, whose credits include The Substance. Beyond the early kiss curls, we’ll see Baker’s sleek side-parted bob, gelled head, and 1940s coiffures, 1950s updos, plus some very dramatic on-stage makeup. Expect some enormous feathered headdresses and glitter decals that became part of her later performance wardrobe. We’ll also surely see the more restrained side of Baker away from the spotlight, as her life took her from cabaret stages into wartime resistance and political activism.

Baker’s appearance evolved alongside her ambitions and her growing cultural influence. For FKA twigs, whose own career has been defined by artistic reinvention, the opportunity is enormous. And judging by this first glimpse, the beauty alone will be worth watching for.
