#6676. Glee Is Getting a Reboot Series 11 Years Later: Everything We Know So Far

Every item on this page was chosen by an ELLE editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

Glee has always held a special place in Ryan Murphy’s heart, so when he heard the show was having a major resurgence on social media, it planted the seeds for a reboot in his mind.

“That show is interesting because it’s come back around,” he said in a July interview with People. “So many young people now watch it. And I’m like, ‘Maybe we should revisit that show.’ My nostalgia and love for that show is enough that I’m like, ‘Well, maybe people would like to see a new incarnation of that in some capacity.’ So yeah, I love that show, and I loved what it became and what it meant to so many people.”

Months later, Murphy delivered on his comments—on October 21, Disney+ and Hulu granted a series order for Glee, 17 years after the original show’s premiere and 11 years after the final episode. The series also announced the news on its official Instagram, writing, “It’s official. Glee is returning.”

Details about the reboot are currently sparse, but here’s everything we know so far.

Yes. In September, Murphy told Entertainment Tonight that there has been progress with writing the show. “We have a script. Brad [Falchuk], Ian [Brennan], and I, who wrote all the first two seasons, have written something,” he said.

The original cast of Glee included Lea Michele, Kevin McHale, Chris Colfer, Darren Criss, Jane Lynch, Amber Riley, Jenna Ushkowitz, Dianna Agron, Heather Morris, Matthew Morrison, Mark Salling, Jonathan Groff, Chord Overstreet, and Harry Shum Jr. Cory Monteith and Naya Rivera were also part of the original cast, but died in 2013 and 2020, respectively.

While Murphy did not state which stars he has been talking to, he told Entertainment Tonight that he’s “been in touch with around 10 of the original cast members. It’s very sweet, and they all had a lot of questions, but they all were very enthusiastic about the idea.”

Hours after the reboot news was revealed, Variety reported that Michele will reportedly join the cast of the reboot. “She’s in,” a source told the outlet, while a second source added, “It’s still early-ish days, but it feels good and we’re happy to get the band back together.” Murphy and Michele did not provide a comment.

Following the news, Morris hinted that she’d be stepping back into Brittany S. Pierce’s cheerleading uniform. “Yes ladies and gentle men of women, rumors are true. Brittany S Pierce was in fact lost in the sewers for all these years. But I’m here to inform you that she is alive and well…and back for more #Glee,” she captioned a throwback photo of herself from the set.

While the post feels like a confirmation, Murphy has not confirmed any of the cast members who will return for the show.

Overstreet and McHale also hinted that they’d be returning. Overstreet wrote, “reunited and fit feels so good!” after the reboot news dropped. McHale reacted to a tweet that said Drake has surpassed the Glee cast with the most Billboard Hot 100 chart entries. “Challenge accepted,” he replied to the tweet.

On October 23, Deadline offered an update on Morris’s and Overstreet’s statuses. The outlet reported that they were in talks to join the reboot.

During his November 11 appearance on The Daily Beast’s Obsessed podcast, Colfer revealed that he’s planning to have more “conversations” about potentially joining the reboot.

He added, “It was really hard going back to the show after Cory passed, and I’m sure it’d be really difficult, especially now that Naya’s gone too,” Colfer said. “But I guess you have to think, are you going to let the loss of two people you love very much prevent you from being around a dozen other people you love as well? There’s a lot to think about with it.”

Colfer does have ideas on what his character, Kurt Hummel, would be up to in the current timeline, though. “I would love to see him like a Miranda Priestly-type, running his own fashion blog or a magazine,” he shared. “I could also see him on tour with Chappell Roan, styling her. There’s a lot of fun avenues they could explore.”

Over the years, several cast members have shared their reactions to a potential Glee reboot, with some stating they would not return to the series if it were made.

Michele, who played the show’s central main character, Rachel Berry, told E! News in September that she’d be open to following Murphy if he expanded the Glee universe. “I love Glee, I will always love Glee,” she said. “I love Ryan Murphy; it holds such a special place in my heart for me, so I will follow Ryan wherever he goes.”

Colfer told Bustle in an interview earlier this month that Glee “was a really tough show to do, and it would be really hard to do it now that Naya [Rivera] is gone.” He added, “I do know that Glee fans would probably come after me with pitchforks and jazz hands if I said no.”

Lynch reflected on her Glee character, Sue Sylvester, in an interview with Entertainment Tonight earlier this month and confirmed that she would join the cast again in a heartbeat. “I would be in like that,” she said.

In May 2025, Riley, who starred as Mercedes Jones, said that she wouldn’t be interested in returning to Glee during her appearance on Monét X Change’s Monét Talks podcast.

“I just feel like what we did was so phenomenal, I don’t want to risk trying to reinvent the wheel,” she said. “Now if they redo it, I think that’s amazing, because there are so many kids now that are just now discovering Glee, and so I think that that’d be really dope. But, you know, we lost cast members. I just feel like the chemistry, that formula, was so specific, and it’s changed now, so I don't know if it would be as effective. I’m always prepared for that question.”

Morris (Brittany S. Pierce) shared in a 2024 interview that she would be down to join the reboot if it were made. “I would,” she said in a video interview. “I think the film industry has come a long way. It was a really tough show to do, and I think being in the space that I’m [in] now, absolutely. I yearn so bad to be in a musical again.”

In 2023, Criss (Blaine Anderson) discussed a potential reboot and revealed that he would be on the fence about it.

“I’m not against it. I know people would like that. I think what made Glee so special is where it sat in its specific time and place,” he explained during his PeopleCon appearance. “I think a lot of cultural moments are defined by the alchemy of where we’re at as a society, and the way it called and responded to each other made it really special.”

Criss continued, “While I, as a fan of Glee, would go, ‘Yeah, I would love to see more,’ I do think there’s something we have to remember about the why, when, and how [the show was] special being very specific to one time. I wouldn’t be against it, but I’m also not screaming to do it. I’m somewhere in between. They have to make it really count.”

At AdoptTogether’s annual Los Angeles Baby Ball in 2022, Ushkowitz (Tina Cohen-Chang) told E! News that she would be open to a reboot if the right team worked together to bring it to life.

“If Ryan was doing it and the right people were involved,” she told the outlet at the time. “I would consider it.” She also dispelled rumors of drama between members of the cast, adding, “We’re a family—families don’t always have to get along. When we were working together, it took more energy to fight than it did to just get along. I spent more hours with them than literally, my own family.”

#6675. Best Men’s Winter Parkas 2026: 17 Heavy-Duty Snow-Busting Coats

The best men's parka is a lot like an upright sleeping bag, except it doesn't simply keep you insulated. It also protects your frostbite-prone fits from Mother Nature’s icy clutches, and keeps you looking sharp in the process. Don't believe us? Just ask the parka's most loyal servant: Oasis frontman Liam Gallagher.

Before giving you our favourites, some quick history: Parkas originated in the Arctic, where the Inuit designed them to withstand bone-chilling temperatures. They then made their way to the US military with the introduction of the N-3B parka in the 1950s. Throughout its evolution, the parka's mission has remained unchanged: to keep not just your torso warm, but your thighs and rear end too. Seriously, you've already worn that waist-length puffer to death: Make like Justin Jefferson. Go long.

The North Face McMurdo down parka isn’t just another winter coat—it’s a cold-weather icon with Antarctic-level credibility. Named after McMurdo Station, the US research hub in Antarctica, this parka is designed to thrive in below-freezing temperatures while keeping you comfortable and protected. With 600-fill recycled down insulation and windproof, waterproof, and breathable DryVent technology, it’s eco-friendly armor for the tundra—or the Target parking lot. Made from recycled nylon and polyester, it’s part of The North Face’s recycled-repurpose collection, combining sustainability with serious performance.

Loaded with features like six exterior pockets, a removable faux-fur ruff, an adjustable hood, and a draft flap, this 3.5-pound powerhouse is your portable fortress of warmth. Stylish touches like the midnight petrol color elevate it above standard winter fare, while practical details make it indispensable for everything from scraping windshields to tackling arctic adventures. Whether you’re braving brutal weather or commuting in comfort, the McMurdo is built to last—complete with The North Face’s warranty to keep it in the game longer than your ever-disappearing gloves.

Mountain Hardwear has been a staple in the outdoor gear world long before its sold-out collaboration with Stüssy (though they’ve probably gained a few new fans in the process). Founded in 1993 in Richmond, California, the brand spun off from the well-known outdoor company Sierra Designs. A group of designers and engineers left Sierra Designs to create Mountain Hardwear, and 32 years later, it’s still famous for its technical outerwear, sleeping bags, and pioneering use of Gore-Tex.

This jacket is built for camping, featuring a durable ripstop shell and 650-fill down. With a fully adjustable insulated hood and a drawcord at the waist to trap in heat, it’s tough to top even before you encounter the two BYO-bevvy pockets—specially designed to carry your favorite beverages. Whether you're in your tent or Air Streamer, this jacket keeps you warm—and your drinks cold—so you can stay cozy and hydrated in style.

Woolrich: So good it doesn't need a logo patch. The American outdoor company was founded in 1830, and since then has become the destination for warmth-minded men who don't need anyone else to know they're walking around in the very best materials.

Which isn't to say this parka won't turn some heads. New for this season, it comes in seven colors, from a stunning light blue to nutty falcon brown, and also boasts some envy-inducing hand-warmer pockets, hidden rib-knit cuffs, and even a water-repellent finish. (A nice touch for a style that typically is more preoccupied with keeping out the cold than the wet.) One more thing: It's called the Cloud because it's incredibly light, even with a 90/10 duck down fill. A winter coat that wears like a summer-weight hoodie? Worth the investment.

This is the kind of Canada Goose jacket that reminds you why the brand is so much more than just a status symbol for finance guys. (Though I'm sure they don't mind being that too.) For one, it's done away with that ubiquitous blue and red logo, and replaced it with a more understated, tonal patch. But that's actually the only thing that's been stripped back here: Otherwise, this parka is packed full of features, from ribbed knit cuffs, to pockets everywhere you look, to a bevy of insulation considerations, from the 625 Fill Down interior all the way to the soft, lined chin guard—a nice touch.

Available this season in Black, Olive, and Desert Sand (above), it's backed by Canada Goose's lifetime guarantee. So, yes, you're spending a fortune. But the brand stands ready to make sure you'll never need to buy another parka again.

The Japanese label FrizmWORKS has reimagined a classic, ‘60s‐era expedition parka silhouette—quilted down, hard-wearing cotton-blend shell, boxy hooded cut—and, sixty years later, given it a whole new life. From the tonal matte finish to the utilitarian drawcord hem, this is a mountain‐camp relic reimagined for your 2025 commute. It’s rugged without resorting to SSX Tricky branding, and along with the requisite down filling also has two fun, unexpected and large pockets on the back. It also comes in a joyful orange color, if that black is a little too subtle for you.

I can't be the only one who was excited to see Reigning Champ get back into making real clothes. (Though, let’s be honest, the brand’s sweatsuits are still some of my favorites.) But this high-powered, goose-filled nylon parka? It's built for Canadian winters, which means it’ll easily thrive anywhere else, too. Technically, that means 700 fill power down, and a weather-repellent nylon shell to keep out wind and rain, as well as the colder temps. Its defining feature is its stealthy, all-black appearance, and Reigning Champ has leant hard into that vibe, with hidden interior pockets, concealed rib cuffs, and a shock cord hood that you can pull as tight as you like. Now you see me, now you don't.

The new kids on the parka block, Big Rock Candy Mountaineering, are bringing the fun back with their vibrant, winter parka colors. These extreme cold-weather parkas take inspiration from mid-century American outdoor brands. Can’t think of any off the top of your head? Skim through a book like this, and you’ll catch the vibe.

BRCM’s parkas are packed with cozy duck down and feature a 100% grosgrain shell. This ribbed texture, courtesy of its tight weave, makes the fabric tough as nails and resistant to wear and tear. The ginormous pockets? Perfect for stashing your winter accessories (or your snacks). And if the wind has you feeling like it’s got something to prove, just tighten up the drawstring waist, hood, and hem. One of the coolest features? The jacket’s silhouette. When cinched, you can clasp your bag around the waist—ideal for those who love a good backpacking adventure. Although BRCM is still a fresh face in the outerwear world, it already feels like an instant classic.

Getting your hands on one of the first-ever parkas is basically impossible—right up there with finding your keys when you’re already late. Enter The Real McCoy’s, which somehow pulls it off with museum-grade reproductions. Every detail is obsessively dialed, down to the DuPont-developed nylon shell that helped kick off the whole modern-materials era.

Today’s outdoor companies are still trying to capture Patagonia’s lightning-in-a-bottle formula from when the brand first burst onto the scene: Be nice to everyone, make products the right way, and design jackets built to last forever. Take its Glacier parka, for example: it’s weatherproof, cozy enough to double as a sleeping bag, and so comfortable you might consider skipping the tent altogether.

If you’re after a quieter, minimalist parka—and you’ve got the budget—the Therme Parka delivers. It’s hip-length, packed with goose down, and built with the brand’s more environmentally friendly GORE-TEX ePE fabric, meaning it’s primed to handle a lifetime of winters.

The Alpha Industries N-3B is the real-deal snorkel parka—because it is the real deal. Produced early in the company's history in the 1950s, the parka is still tough as nails and loaded with reinforced elbow patches, a full-length storm flap, and snug inset knit cuffs that keep wind firmly in its place.

Founded in 1960, Fjällräven are sort of Sweden's Patagonia. By which we mean they've always thought about three things: High-performance materials, a reasonable enough price point, and dressing it all up in some great primary colors.

Nanga is your favorite outerwear brand’s favorite outerwear brand. Its parka riffs on the US Air Force’s N-3B flight jacket, upgraded with AuroraTex—a high-performance fabric that keeps you dry no matter what. Add handwarmer pockets and a discreet cigar pouch, and you’ve got a parka that nails the perfect blend between utility and style.

Goldwin is so good, it literally owns the North Face in Japan. (Like, literally.) This handsome down parka is wind-blocking, body-warming, and equipped with a PERTEX Quantum ripstop lining (and shell) to prevent the tears and rips that lightweight fabrics can otherwise be prone to.

Berghaus' Meru jacket—which is long enough to qualify as a parka in our book—is packed with retro styling, from the color blocks to the cinchable waistband. 2L Gore-Tex means you could wear it up any peak, but its general aura means you could also wear it up on stage, hands behind your back, tambourine on your head.

Montbell's mastery of lightweight, easy-to-rock, nicely-priced outdoors gear has become its calling card, and it’s on full display here. This down parka is easy to incorporate into pretty much any wardrobe, and even has some nice-looking stitching (which, by the way, the heads call ‘baffling’).

What do you get when you cross a parka with a fireman jacket? A full-scale compliment magnet.

First and foremost: functionality. A great parka should incorporate more features than a midnight infomercial. In the outer shell, you’ll typically find materials like nylon or polyester, and sometimes more rugged options like Gore-Tex. But it's also worth peeking under the hood—literally. Parkas are usually filled with down (duck or goose feathers) or synthetic insulation like polyester. Down is warm and lightweight, but it’s the fair-weather friend of insulation—it falters when wet. Synthetic insulations, on the other hand, is the ride-or-die option, keeping you warm even when soggy.

Hoods are another essential feature. Most will be made of a weatherproof fabric, and some come equipped with fluffy genuine- or faux-fur trims that gently tickle your face with a touch of winter luxury. And then there are the pockets—no one wants to walk around in a blizzard with frozen fingers. (Look for fleece linings.) Finally, asses the length. Longer parkas offer more warmth and protection from the elements, while shorter ones are perfect for commuters who need to dodge frostbite without overheating on the subway.

While function is the defining characteristic of a good parka, a great one should also give your winter fits a serious upgrade. Pair it with a thermal and a chunky sweater for a no-brainer look, or go bold by layering it over a denim jacket, adding corduroys, and anchoring with sturdy boots.

Style is subjective, we know—that’s the fun of it. But we’re serious about helping our audience get dressed. Whether it’s the best white sneakers, the flyest affordable suits, or the need-to-know menswear drops of the week, GQ Recommends’ perspective is built on years of hands-on experience, an insider awareness of what’s in and what’s next, and a mission to find the best version of everything out there, at every price point.

Our staffers aren’t able to try on every single piece of clothing you read about on GQ.com (fashion moves fast these days), but we have an intimate knowledge of each brand’s strengths and know the hallmarks of quality clothing—from materials and sourcing, to craftsmanship, to sustainability efforts that aren’t just greenwashing. GQ Recommends heavily emphasizes our own editorial experience with those brands, how they make their clothes, and how those clothes have been reviewed by customers. Bottom line: GQ wouldn’t tell you to wear it if we wouldn’t.

We make every effort to cast as wide of a net as possible, with an eye on identifying the best options across three key categories: quality, fit, and price.

To kick off the process, we enlist the GQ Recommends braintrust to vote on our contenders. Some of the folks involved have worked in retail, slinging clothes to the masses; others have toiled for small-batch menswear labels; all spend way too much time thinking about what hangs in their closets.

We lean on that collective experience to guide our search, culling a mix of household names, indie favorites, and the artisanal imprints on the bleeding-edge of the genre. Then we narrow down the assortment to the picks that scored the highest across quality, fit, and price.

Across the majority of our buying guides, our team boasts firsthand experience with the bulk of our selects, but a handful are totally new to us. So after several months of intense debate, we tally the votes, collate the anecdotal evidence, and emerge with a list of what we believe to be the absolute best of the category right now, from the tried-and-true stalwarts to the modern disruptors, the affordable beaters to the wildly expensive (but wildly worth-it) designer riffs.

Whatever your preferences, whatever your style, there's bound to be a superlative version on this list for you. (Read more about GQ's testing process here.)

#6674. Baked Feta Bites

Baked feta pasta took the world by storm, and once we tried it, we knew we couldn’t stop at just the classic viral recipe. We created these baked feta bites to be the perfect no-fuss holiday appetizer, capturing all of the same flavors as the OG. Thanks to easy, store-bought ingredients, these flaky, flavor-packed bites are perfect for any last-minute party planning.

The puff pastry:Puff pastry can be a game-changer in appetizer recipes, and selecting the right one is essential. Because your choice of puff pastry determines the overall texture, we recommend opting for as high a quality as you can find. Brands like Taste of Inspirations, Pepperidge Farm, or Dufour offer excellent options that guarantee a delicate, flaky crust that will elevate your bites to a whole new level of perfection.

Speaking of, we understand that achieving flawlessly cut squares can be a daunting task. Here’s a quick guide to ensure your squares are uniform: On a lightly floured surface, roll out the puff pastry sheets, smoothing out any creases. Using a chef’s knife, cut your pastry in half crosswise, then each piece in half crosswise again, so you have 4 strips of pastry. Cut those in half lengthwise, then cut each piece into 3 squares, until you have 24 squares.

How to make baked feta bites:Once you’ve got your pastry squares, you can begin assembling your bites, starting with greasing a mini muffin tin with cooking spray. Gently press each square into the prepared cups, allowing the pastry to protrude slightly—this subtle bump will transform into a beautifully cupped shape during baking. Then add in your dollop of jam, shallots, a piece of roasted red pepper, a cube of feta (crumbled feta is perfectly fine too!), and a touch of thyme. We love these as is, but feel free to switch things up if you like—who knows, you might just discover a new flavor combo you’ll make again and again.

Storage & make ahead:Wondering about leftovers? Worry not. These baked feta bites are just as delightful the next day. Store them in an airtight container in the refrigerator, and when you’re ready for another flavor-packed moment, simply reheat them in the oven to restore their crispiness. Want to make these way ahead of time? Bake these, let them cool, and then place them in a freezer-safe bag before storing in the freezer for up to 3 months.

#6671. Restaurant Booths Are Back—and Better Than Ever

“When I walk into a restaurant and see a worn-in bright red-and-white striped booth, I already know it’s going to be good,” says Anna Albury, designer and writer behind Cool Stuff NYC, the cult-followed newsletter she curates with her husband, Garrett. She, like many booth loyalists, can wax poetic about her favorite seats in the city, citing the coat-rack-clad booths of Cobble Hill’s Long Island Bar, Le Veau d’Or’s cherry-red banquettes on the Upper East Side, and Carroll Gardens newcomer Trudie’s, which features charming two-top booths.

While booths have long been considered the “best seat in the house,” there was a time in the not-so-distant past when business diners preferred private dining rooms and social diners sought out communal tables. But there’s good news for booth lovers like Albury: this past year has brought on a booth boom of never-before-seen proportions. Restaurants, hotels, and members’ clubs of all distinctions are installing booths and banquettes by the mile. From design-forward diners like London-based Supernova to fine dining institutions like the Roman and Williams–designed Marcel and swanky cocktail lounges like Andres Diaz’s newly opened Bar Leone, without a doubt, booths are back.

Mohair-upholstered booths are a key feature of the newly opened Marcel restaurant in New York, designed by Roman and Williams.

Interior designers who cater to hospitality venues are seeing the shift in demand firsthand. “Across daytime and evening-only restaurant projects, clients are coming in with booths already on the brief, more as a starting point than an afterthought,” says Sarita Posada, whose eponymous New York City-based design firm is behind some of the hottest tables in Paris and London, including the aforementioned Supernova, as well as Cherry and 74 Duke. “I think people are a little fatigued overall on overexposure, whether that be digitally or when they go out,” she adds, citing booths as a way to carve out your own piece of real estate in a room.

It wasn’t all that long ago that communal tables reigned supreme as the seating setup du jour. David Prior, founder of the editorial-led travel company Prior, cites the farm-to-table movement and food leaders like Alice Waters as popularizing long communal tables roughly from 2009 to 2016. He also points to Jim Denevan’s beloved roving dinner series, Outstanding in the Field, which became famous for its extremely long dinner tables.

But this all changed in 2020, when the pandemic transformed how people ate and gathered. During that period—and the 18 months that followed—private dining became the default. “People wanted to be hermetically sealed,” says Prior with a laugh.

Sleek leather booths at Le Cafe Nac in London, designed by Sarita Posada Interiors.

Now, Prior says that he’s seeing what he calls an “alone-together moment,” and booth seating sits perfectly within that larger movement. “We want to have our intimate moments, but we also want to feel that we’re part of a similar thing,” he says, citing his recent launch party for his podcast, Traveling Through, where groups of people clustered in booths like small islands within a greater archipelago. “It’s all about connection right now, because people are so disconnected.”

Red leather booths at Bar Primi Penn District, designed by Meyer Davis.

Cafe Zaffri, the stylish Mediterranean restaurant within The Twenty Two members’ club in Union Square, is one such setting known to welcome the power lunch crowd in its sumptuous horseshoe booths. “People still want to experience the energy of a lively dining room, but they also want space for real conversation and connection,” says Leigh Salem, a partner at Post Company, whose firm designed the space.

Velvet booths at Cafe Zaffri, inside the New York outpost of The Twenty Two.

From a design perspective, booths also add a sense of storiedness to a space. “There’s something about the memory and history they carry in great, old rooms like Bemelmans Bar or Minetta Tavern,” says Posada, who installed booths in two of her recent restaurant projects to infuse the rooms with intimacy and nostalgia.

But today’s booths are adding a modern twist. At Supernova, Posada drew inspiration from 1970s American diners but made the space cinematic with careful restraint on color—keeping to chrome, black, and butter yellow. In Auric Room 1915, the members-only supper club and speakeasy at Lone Mountain Ranch in Big Sky, cowhide booths bring levity to the space while staying entirely on brand. And how could one miss the chocolate-brown banquettes at Marcel in the iconic Breuer building that made the rounds on Instagram with its buzzy opening?

A ’70s twist on the booth at Supernova in London, designed by Sarita Posada Interiors.

More than just contributing to a feeling, booths add functionality. At the beloved West Village institution Demo, booths were “one of the best ways to utilize a narrow pathway,” says co-owner Jacob Nass. In Bufon, the team’s second restaurant, the perimeter of the dining room is lined with blue banquettes, creating an almost conversation-pit feel.

While booths might look simple, designing one is more technical than one might think. Davis notes it’s important to consider how seating supports different dining durations, service styles, and group sizes and says that the firm carefully evaluates material durability, placement, and seat height when installing a booth. “We use a range of booth typologies which include perimeter banquettes that define a room’s edge, curved or semi-enclosed booths, and integrated seating that becomes part of the architectural millwork.” All of this is in service of supporting the overall design concept.

Outdoor booths are a key feature of the Tatjana von Stein–designed Hotel Corazon in Mallorca.

Booths work in the most serious and stately of spaces, as well as the most fun. Hotel Corazon, the beloved Mallorca hotel run by fashion photographer Kate Bellm and her husband, artist Edgar Lopez, installed bespoke round booths last spring in its revamped restaurant. “The intention was to create a space that feels intimate, warm, and relaxed, while retaining a sense of playfulness,” says designer Tatjana von Stein, who brought the space to life with circular booths crafted from powder-coated metal and made in Portugal with the hotel’s sun motif. “We wanted guests to feel comfortable lingering, connecting, and enjoying the convivial spirit that sits at the heart of Hotel Corazon.”

At One4One, the chic sports bar opened by Dylan Hales and Ronnie Flynn, booths are part of the owners’ broader mission to “create a true local hang.” At The Flower Shop, their first foray into hospitality, there’s a brass plaque above the corner booth that reads “Captain’s Quarters,” reserving it for friends and family.

The expansive, warmly lit booths at One4One.

As you might imagine, securing one of the highly sought-after seats at One4One or The Flower Shop isn’t something the owners take lightly. “A booth creates comfort and, in a way, commitment. You get a booth when you mean it. When you’re settling in for the night, waiting for more people to join, and really planting your flag in a place,” says Flynn. “That is, if you’re lucky enough to snag one.”

#6670. Homemade Cranberry Sauce

I don’t care if you love it or hate it—cranberry sauce is a Thanksgiving STAPLE. Personally, I love it. Every year, you can find me spooning multiple helpings of the sweet-tart sauce onto my plate to balance out all of the rich savory dishes. While I understand the nostalgic appeal of the canned stuff, homemade cranberry sauce is 1,000x better. It's fresh, versatile, and so easy to make. All you need are 5 ingredients and 20 minutes to make this staple holiday side.

What People Are Saying:“This is the simplest, but tastiest cranberry sauce i’ve ever made… My family loved it so much, i’ve had to make several batches for christmas gifts, per request.” -OrangeSushi

“Made this for Thanksgiving, and everyone loved it, including the ones that don’t care for cranberry sauce!! I added some fresh mandarin oranges and cinnamon to mine. Everyone wanted leftovers to take home! We put it in our oatmeal with pecans for breakfast in the morning! I plan to make this all year round instead of just at Thanksgiving! ❤️” -RedDice

First, grab a small saucepan—but not just any saucepan! Make sure it’s either stainless steel or enameled cast-iron. Whatever you do, avoid aluminum, which will react with the copious acid in the berries, giving the sauce an unpleasant metallic taste. Add the sugar and 1 c. water and stir until the sugar is dissolved. Now add the cranberries and bring the mixture to a boil over medium-high heat.

The beauty of cranberries is that (1) they readily burst and release their juices, and (2) their juices have so much natural pectin that the berries thicken nearly to jam in mere minutes. Ten minutes of simmering, with some occasional stirring thrown in, is all the cooking required. Don’t sweat it if a small minority of the berries haven’t burst—they probably will by the time the sauce has cooled.

Stir in the orange zest and let the sauce cool; it will continue to thicken. And believe it or not, that really is all there is to it. What’s more, this is a Thanksgiving dish you can get off your plate up to 1 week in advance. Just transfer the cooled cranberry sauce to an airtight container and refrigerate until the big feast. Bonus: The flavors will continue to meld and deepen while it hangs out in the fridge.

The full list of ingredients and directions can be found in the recipe below.

While this version is perfectly classic, if you want to experiment, you’ve got a few options. If your cranberry sauce isn’t complete without orange juice, you can sub freshly squeezed or bottled orange juice for some or all of the water. Alternatively, if you’re averse to oranges, feel free to skip the zest and add a pinch of ground cinnamon or a couple of cinnamon sticks instead. Craving some crunch? Throw in some chopped pecans at the end of cooking.

Check out our keto cranberry sauce if you're looking to satisfy every diet, or our cranberry relish if you want a similar side without having to turn on your stove.

If you have leftovers, store them in an airtight container in the fridge for up to 1 week.

#6667. Steven Spielberg Believes Empathy Is Our ‘Only Real Superpower’

The veteran filmmaker was honored at the 18th annual MoMA Film Benefit with Chanel.

As rain poured down on Manhattan Thursday night, so did the tributes to Steven Spielberg. The veteran director was honored at this year’s MoMA Film Benefit, presented by Chanel, with homages from fellow icons of cinema and collaborators including Martin Scorsese, Tom Cruise, Emily Blunt, and Ariana DeBose. To top off the night, Spielberg (and the crowd) was treated to a surprise acoustic performance by Bruce Springsteen.

Honoring Spielberg’s contributions to film feels like a no-brainer, given the dozens of masterpieces he has delivered in his decades-long career, spanning Jaws, E.T., the Indiana Jones franchise, Schindler’s List, Jurassic Park, Saving Private Ryan, and many more, all the way up to Disclosure Day, which was just released this summer. Reflecting on his latest, Spielberg said in his speech, “It’s less about aliens and more about empathy. Empathy is the only real superpower that humanity possesses. It’s the only form of magic, I think, that exists in the world.”

And while he accepted the honor solo, the director said he shares the recognition with the hundreds of people in his casts and crews, including those who work at craft services. He also took a moment to thank his wife.

“When you honor me, you are also honoring my wife, Kate Capshaw, because the stuff I put in each of my films is from the stuff of life, real life, that Kate and I have created with family, friends, and conversation, and being aware that there’s more to living than just what we do for a living,” he said. “The confidence she’s given me every day for the past 43 years, I would not be the same person, or the same filmmaker, without her central to my very human existence.”

The program included opening remarks from Cruise, who starred in Minority Report and War of the Worlds, followed by a speech from Scorsese, who reflected on his decades of friendship with Spielberg. “Listen, we’ve known each other since 1972—how did we get to be in our eighties? What happened?” he joked. DeBose, who starred in Spielberg’s West Side Story remake and won an Oscar, performed “Somewhere” from the legendary musical.

Blunt, who starred in Disclosure Day, revealed that the back of Spielberg’s director’s chair is labeled with “Dad.” “‘Dad’ still has this childlike enthusiasm, this spontaneity,” she said. And when he’s “happy with a take, you’ll see him, he’ll just come running out of the tent with his fists in the air, and he’s cheering, and it’s like the best damn moment of your career,” she added. Spielberg later returned the praise, saying Blunt “could play any role—including James Bond.”

Steve Martin and Martin Short alternated zippy one-liners while introducing the guest of honor (they even joked about how many awards they shared between the three of them). And Stephen Colbert helped introduce the grand finale, Bruce Springsteen, who sang “Dancing in the Dark” on his guitar. Before jumping into song, The Boss took a moment to say a few words about Spielberg too, recalling the summer when Jaws first came out when he was living on the Jersey Shore. There used to be a tradition called night swimming, where people would swim in the ocean nude, often with someone they were interested in. But ever since Jaws, “Steven Spielberg fucked that up. He fucked it up good,” Springsteen said, to a room of laughter.

Other attendees included Drew Barrymore, Cate Blanchett, Robert De Niro, Jeff Goldblum, Riley Keough, John Krasinski, Donna Langley, Spike Lee, Lorne Michaels, Michelle Pfeiffer, Zoe Saldaña, Francesca Scorsese, Christopher Walken, and Michelle Williams. Jennifer Lawrence and Cooke Maroney made a low-key appearance.

#6661. ELLE Escapes: Río Grande

Every item on this page was chosen by an ELLE editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

Puerto Rico has long been one of my favorite island destinations for a little rest and relaxation. Time and again, I find myself drawn back to the charming towns dotted along its northern and northeastern coasts. This month, my travels brought me to Río Grande, a tranquil, picturesque municipality affectionately known as La Ciudad de El Yunque (The City of El Yunque).

Just a 30-minute drive from Luis Muñoz Marín International Airport, Río Grande offers a calmer setting than the bustling streets of San Juan, while still keeping the capital city’s attractions within easy reach. Beloved for its lush landscapes, breathtaking scenery, and abundant flora and fauna, the area is also home to a significant portion of El Yunque National Forest, which, fun fact, is the only tropical rainforest in the U.S. National Forest System.

Whether you prefer lounging poolside with a piña colada, venturing into the rainforest for a scenic hike, or heading west to meander through the vibrant streets of Old San Juan, I’ve found that Río Grande makes for an idyllic home base to experience the best of what the island has to offer.

Ahead, discover my recommendations for where to stay, what to eat, and what to explore in this enchanting corner of Puerto Rico.

Taking a nature walk or scenic hike through El Yunque National Forest is a must when visiting Río Grande. Whether you book a guided tour or venture out on your own with a rental car, there are trails suited to every experience level. Along the way, you’ll be stunned by the sheer variety of plants and wildlife you encounter. On my trip, I finally put a face to the symphony of chirps I’d been hearing throughout my stay: the Puerto Rican spindalis, a small, yellow-bellied bird native to the island.

The forest is also home to a seemingly endless variety of tropical trees, mushrooms, orchids, and ferns. Climb the spiral staircase of the Yokahú Observation Tower for panoramic views of the lush green canopy and surrounding mountain peaks, and be sure to pack water shoes if you fancy a refreshing dip in one of the forest’s rivers or natural waterfall pools.

Whether you’re an avid golfer or just getting into the sport, Río Grande has several world-class courses worth exploring. Among them is Bahía Beach Golf Club, an 18-hole, par-72 course designed by renowned golf course architect Robert Trent Jones Jr. in 2008. Stretching 6,890 yards through lush tropical landscapes, the course features 15 holes bordering water, with beautiful rainforest views along the way. You’ll wind around scenic lakes before reaching the Atlantic coastline for the final few holes, making for an unforgettable morning or afternoon on the green.

Set sail from the nearby town of Fajardo for a morning, afternoon, or all-day affair spent exploring nearby islands with seemingly untouched beaches. Popular destinations include Culebra and Icacos Island, where you can lounge on the boat, soak up the sun, swim in crystal-clear waters, or snorkel among vibrant coral reefs teeming with colorful fish.

Perla, located at Four Seasons, opened this November under the direction of executive chef Victor Rosado and became one of my favorite dining spots during my visit. Taking its name from the Spanish word for “pearl,” the elegant restaurant offers a tempting selection of small bites, from pillowy Parker House rolls served with smoked butter to spicy salmon mousse, alongside standout seafood dishes like hamachi and Chilean sea bass.

The thoughtfully designed interior boasts natural wood accents and bold contemporary artwork, with sweeping ocean views to admire between courses. As for what to order, don’t miss the oyster brûlée with yuzu kosho hollandaise and crispy Ibérico ham, the prime New York strip steak served with Hasselback potatoes, or the tender octopus accompanied by creamy potato causa.

For lunch, head to Don Pepe, a longtime local favorite where the atmosphere is casual and the focus is on authentic Puerto Rican cooking made with quality ingredients and bold flavors. The menu spans traditional favorites like beef piononos and mofongo served with your choice of protein and sauce, alongside heartier, mouthwatering dishes like succulent grilled pork loin, the restaurant’s signature burger, and lobster risotto. The extensive cocktail menu also offers a tempting selection of tropical concoctions made with locally produced Don Q rum.

Another recent addition to the dining options at the Four Seasons Resort is Ocean Terrace, a picturesque open-air restaurant set along the shoreline. Open for breakfast, lunch, and dinner, the restaurant has a varied menu with something to satisfy every craving.

Mornings begin with a generous breakfast buffet, and if you have a sweet tooth like me, the coquito French toast on the à la carte menu is a must-try. For lunch, you’ll find everything from truffle honey stracciatella served with ciabatta to salads, pizzas, and sandwiches. Come dinnertime, I’d recommend exploring the selection of freshly made pastas, especially the creamy carbonara with pancetta—a dish I’m still dreaming about.

When you’re in the mood for a glamorous, atmospheric lounge to sip cocktails, head to Palm Court. The sleek, modern interior features plush seating that invites you to settle in and unwind, while a grand, square-shaped white marble bar serves as the room’s centerpiece. Beyond the elegant interior, an outdoor terrace offers additional seating for those who prefer to dine or enjoy a drink in the warm ocean breeze.

Located at the Bahía Beach Club, Sugar Beach Bar is a laid-back, open-air spot serving flavorful cocktails and delicious shareable bites. Sip on a tasty tropical cocktail made with local rum or tequila while soaking up stunning views of the ocean waves and Sugar Beach Pool.

Situated right by the Bahía Beach driving range, El Cocoteros Grill is a casual spot to unwind with a local beer. Open for breakfast and lunch, the restaurant offers a relaxed atmosphere, modern furnishings, and scenic rainforest views. And if you’re out on the golf course, you can even have drinks delivered straight to your golf cart.

You can always count on a five-star stay at a Four Seasons, and the recently opened Four Seasons Resort and Residences Puerto Rico, nestled within the picturesque Bahía Beach community, is no exception. Set across 483 acres of spectacular tropical landscape, the resort boasts 104 guest rooms, 35 luxurious suites, and an impressive collection of private residences. The property has rightfully earned a coveted Michelin Key in recognition of its exceptional grounds, hospitality, and dining.

The accommodations are everything you’d expect from the hotel company, with luxe, modern furnishings, 24-hour in-room dining, and an attentive concierge team that can arrange everything from dinner reservations to rainforest excursions. The location also doubles as a private nature reserve, with conservation efforts that include rain gardens and sea turtle nesting protection. Guests can explore the surrounding wildlife and tropical flora through guided nature experiences, all without leaving the vicinity. And if you find yourself wishing you could stay a little longer, the dreamy private residences offer a more permanent escape to paradise.

As for how to spend your days, take your pick among lounging along the resort’s two miles of pristine beachfront, cooling off in one of the two swimming pools, or heading out to explore the island.

A golf lover’s dream, Bahía Beach Resort & Golf Club offers a more residential take on the traditional resort experience. Visitors can enjoy a private getaway in one of the community’s luxurious villas and residences, many of which are available for short-term rentals. Among them is Paradise View Villa, an incredible two-bedroom, three-bathroom property that comes with a six-passenger golf cart for getting around the grounds. Guests also have access to an array of resort amenities, including the golf club, tennis facilities, a fitness center, and the Lakehouse, where a variety of water sports await.

Ideal for families, larger groups, or those planning a special celebration, Wyndham Grand Rio Mar has 400 guest rooms, including 40 spacious suites with refined, colorful furnishings. With so much to see and do on the property, you could easily spend your entire getaway without venturing beyond the resort. Indulge in restorative treatments at El Yunque Spa, spend a lazy afternoon under the sun on the beach, or enjoy a round of golf at the scenic Rio Mar Country Club.

Suitable for beginners and experts alike, this eight-piece kit is a great choice for anyone looking for a fresh start.

“You don’t necessarily need to buy the most expensive set on the market,” Erickson notes. “Affordable makeup brush brands like Real Techniques and Eco Tools are sufficient for those wanting to keep it simple. Assess what you’re doing makeup-wise daily and consider what you actually need.”

Number of brushes: Four (plus two makeup sponges)

Brushes included: All-over eyeshadow brush, blend & crease brush, define & smudge brush

If your current face makeup brushes aren’t cutting it, upgrade to this do-it-all duo from Anisa Beauty. The compact concealer brush fits perfectly under the eyes for a smooth, crease-free finish.

“This set of brushes from Anisa Beauty makes applying my base makeup a dream,” beauty commerce editor Tiffany Dodson Davis says. “Not only are the bristles super soft, but their angled shapes make it easy to blend my foundation and concealer quickly and seamlessly.”

Brushes included: Pinnacle foundation brush, angled concealer brush

What Are the Best Makeup Brushes Worth Shopping?

According to Erickson, the most essential makeup brushes in your set are the ones you use with powder products, such as bronzer, blush, or setting powder. "Everyone should own a small powder brush—or even something that resembles a large eyeshadow brush—to cut shine where needed and set concealer. An angled brush can be helpful when using bronzer or contour, as well as a medium-sized cheek brush for powder blush."

And when it comes to eye makeup brushes, the expert adds, "It can be helpful to have a dual-sided angled brush-spoolie combo for brows, as well as for winged liner. A small, dense, pointed brush for the lash line and inner corner is nice to have, as well as one or two blending brushes for the eyelids."

Should I Opt for Synthetic or Natural Bristles?

"I like to say there is nothing 'natural' about animal hair," Anisa Telwar Kaicker tells Bazaar. "It can dry faster and break more quickly. Man-made synthetics can be long-lasting, hygienic, innovative in shape, and soft to the touch."

Erickson agrees that synthetic makeup brushes outperform products made using animal by-products. "Synthetic brushes tend to be more durable and last longer. Less and less natural bristles areused today, and as a makeup artist, I don’t think we need them, performance-wise."

What’s the Most Effective Way to Clean Makeup Brushes?

"When I deep clean my makeup brushes once or twice a month, I typically use Dr. Bronner’s 18-in-1 castile soap," Erickson notes. "At the very least, use a quick-dry brush cleaner like Sephora’s Daily Brush Cleaner between each use to avoid the spread of bacteria."

Telwar Kaicker suggests that after deep cleaning, you remove excess water from your brushes with a towel. Then, tilt the brush downward to prevent water from seeping into the ferrule and breaking down the glue in the brush head.

How Often Should I Replace My Makeup Brushes?

According to Erickson, high-quality, well-cared-for brushes can last for years. "If it ain’t broke, don’t fix it. I’ve had some of my makeup brushes last a decade and some only last a year or two. If you love it and you’re able to properly sanitize it, use it for as long as you can."

How do you know when it's time for a new set? Erickson says it all comes down to the glue. "Typically, when a makeup brush goes bad, the glue between the brush and handle starts to break down due to wear and moisture from cleaning. When that happens, toss it and move on. For beauty blenders and sponges that harbor bacteria, toss them after a few uses, no matter how well you sanitize them. Toss after a few uses, especially if you’re acne-prone."

#6659. ‘Clothing Has Impact’: Zoe Latta, Kat Typaldos, and Turner on Styling Los Angeles Mayor-Elect Nithya Raman

When Nithya Raman stepped onto the podium for her first press conference as the newly minted mayor-elect of Los Angeles, keen eyes might have clocked her “if you know, you know” attire—specifically, a vintage tangerine Narciso Rodriguez motorcycle jacket and a pair of Eckhaus Latta jeans. Throughout much of her political career as a two-term LA councilwoman, Raman had deployed the classic conventions of a local representative: a sturdy button-down shirt here, a matching pantsuit there. Her more fashion-forward transformation in recent months comes courtesy of an unlikely political styling trio: fashion designer Zoe Latta (of bicoastal cool-kid brand Eckhaus Latta) and celebrity stylists Kat Typaldos and Turner.

No matter which way you cut a pantsuit, female politicians are often boxed in by frustrating parameters. Style is confined to restrained silhouettes barely spiced up by the addition of a pussy-bow blouse. And while policy is more important than Prada, Latta, Typaldos, and Turner found plenty of ways to change what’s expected of a candidate’s wardrobe. As Typaldos put it candidly: “If one more person says ‘bold, colorful suit’ for a powerful woman, I will throw my computer out of the window.”

Mayor-elect Nithya Raman at her first press conference post-win in a Narciso Rodriguez leather jacket from The RealReal and Eckhaus Latta jeans

The cohort connected with Raman’s cause via their mutual LA friend Chas McCarty, a restaurateur and man-about-town. Latta recalls: “It was in the back of Botanica [a local restaurant, where Raman was holding a campaign gathering]. I had my baby with me, and the binky fell out, and Nithya was mid sentence and got up from the table, got under the table, grabbed the binky, continuing to talk about small businesses and handed it to me, and I was just like, This woman has my book—whatever she needs.”

In the weeks following Raman’s surprise bid against incumbent mayor Karen Bass, a wardrobe shift wasn’t exactly at the top of her to-do list. In those early days, Raman wore what Latta affectionately described as “a lot of capes,” but her sartorial traditionalism—and prior lack of a styling team—was part of her appeal. “She wasn’t doing anything wrong—she had other things to do,” Latta says. The task at hand: to give her wardrobe a little zhuzh. “She wears clothes really well. It is a treat to get to dress her, and she enjoys it. And that, to me, is so fundamental. It’s not in a peacocking way.”

Voting day: Cleo Camp top and Altuzarra skirt from The RealReal

Latta, Typaldos, and Turner are all used to working with powerful women but in a different arena of celebrity. The one thing they did know about dressing a prospective mayor: a subtle, sustainable approach was best. This included plenty of vintage and secondhand shopping from The RealReal, as well as local designers, casually blended with her preexisting wardrobe. Such fashionable thriftiness not only fit Raman’s grounded style but also spoke to the trio’s sensibilities as self-employed small-business owners. “I’m thinking about [the client], the context, the world that they live in,” Turner says. “Kat is probably similar in that we’re thinking about how to make them shine in this world. And so you’re taking into consideration who they are, what they are. You’re doing your research.”

Raman at her election party in a plum Erdem from The RealReal

Unsurprisingly, there was no high-glamour, full-look policy here. Instead, they took a little-bit-of-this, little-bit-of-that approach to arrive at looks that felt authentic. It could be a white Akris blouse, a plum Erdem dress, or a burnt orange Altuzarra leather skirt paired with a long-sleeve shirt from LA-based designer Cleo Camp. Yes, there were suits, like the one from J.Crew that Raman wore to debate Bass, but all were items a constituent would want in their own workwear closet. “In that process, we watched Nithya develop agency about what to wear and how clothing can empower,” Typaldos says. “For me, what was cool is that she’s such a denim person, and I trust nobody more [than the person] wearing a striped shirt and a denim and a loafer. Clothing has that impact. How can you make it feel like a second skin enough?”

Raman debates incumbent mayor Karen Bass in a J.Crew suit.

When it comes to dressing a politician like Raman, unlike a musician or an actor, there’s no calling in favors. The mayor-to-be couldn’t take so much as a friends-and-family discount from Latta’s own brand, nor was she interested in splurging on outlandish pieces. If it were otherwise, fashion would be an even bigger point of contention for opponents looking to undercut her platform. Case in point: Following New York City mayor Zohran Mamdani’s inauguration, his wife Rama Duwaji’s borrowed and rented designer items drew much discussion, with their brand names and price tags splashed across rage-bait headlines in the New York Post. In a feature with The Cut published the month before, the fashion credits unusually made it explicit that the clothing was on loan from the designers, despite that being standard behind-the-scenes editorial procedure.

Latta, Typaldos, and Turner have never worked as a styling trio before. They attribute their banding together in part to Raman’s ability to build community. “She really does bring people together,” Turner says. “I haven’t worked with another stylist or designer in this capacity, but it was thoroughly enjoyable to be in the presence of powerful women just trying to help another woman rise up. I think it’ll probably be my most important work to date.”

#6651. Safe Word: The Best Jewelry Launches of November 2026

Safe Word is a series highlighting the latest trends in the jewelry market, keeping you up to date on all things that sparkle and shine.

November’s jewelry launches are looking both backward and forward, with designers revisiting their roots, reworking archival ideas, and stepping into entirely new territory. First up, Quentin Jones is taking her surrealist art off the wall and onto the body with ‘Nocturne’, her first jewelry collection; Pomellato reaches back to 1997 to revive “Moneta Orientale” as a colorful modern talisman; David Yurman celebrates the magic of a New York holiday with Michael B. Jordan, Yerin Ha, and Inde Navarrette; Vhernier revisits its iconic “Trottola” design with new proportions and contrasting materials; Di Volpe reinterprets the classic tennis bracelet with customizable gemstones in “DiSegno”; Brent Neale transforms the classic bow into sculptural fine jewelry with “Wrap It Up”; and Kendra Scott launches the new “Kendra Scott Collection,” reimagining her signature Spike motif as a personal talisman. From archival revivals and meaningful motifs to innovative designs and new creative directions, November’s launches prove that sometimes the best way forward starts with looking back. For the rest of the month, we’ve got you covered on all the jewelry-related happenings worth knowing about.

Quentin Jones is taking her art off the wall and onto the body with “Nocturne,” the first jewelry collection from House of Quentin Jones. Following the multidisciplinary artist’s debut of surrealist ceramics and tapestries last year, the new collection transforms recurring gestures and symbols from her work into sculptural collars, cuffs, armbands, pendants, chains, and earrings. Eyes, hands, stars, moons, tears, and knots take shape in silver and gold vermeil alongside freshwater pearls, onyx, opals, jade, glass, and silk tassels, giving the pieces a dreamlike, talismanic quality. Beginning as drawings and hand collages in Jones’s Brooklyn studio, each design carries her surrealist visual language into wearable form, further blurring the line between art, design, and fashion.

Kendra Scott Launches an Eponymous Collection

Kendra Scott is offering a more personal look into her design world with the launch of the “Kendra Scott Collection,” a new line spanning fashion and fine jewelry. Its first edition, “The Spike,” revisits a silhouette the designer has worn throughout her career as a personal symbol of strength, confidence, and conviction. Inspired by nature and the radiance of the night sky, the collection translates the pointed motif into sculptural necklaces, earrings, bracelets, and charms, balancing bold proportions with intricate craftsmanship. Fashion jewelry incorporates tiger’s eye, malachite, and turquoise, while fine jewelry introduces lab-grown diamonds, pavé detailing, labradorite, and lapis. From statement-making links to delicate diamond charms, the collection offers a new interpretation of Scott’s longtime signature, inviting wearers to make the symbol their own.

Alison Lou’s ‘New Wave’ Collection Experiments With New Materials

Alison Lou is entering a new chapter with “New Wave,” a fine jewelry collection that introduces unexpected materials and a fresh approach to the designer’s signature playful aesthetic. Exploring the relationship between movement and form, the collection pairs lightweight titanium and ceramic with lab-grown diamonds, creating fluid, sculptural silhouettes that curve and catch the light. Available in Fig and Denim Blue colorways, the designs include wavy rings, diamond-accented signets, delicate thread necklaces, and statement drop earrings. With its unconventional materials and easy-to-wear designs, “New Wave” brings a new sense of movement to Alison Lou’s everyday jewelry.

Jenny Bird and Emese Gormley Partner on the Anyu Ring

Jenny Bird is expanding her JB FINE collection with a new collaboration featuring lifestyle creator and Lipstick on the Rim podcast host Emese Gormley. Named in honor of Gormley’s mother, the Anyu Ring offers a personal take on the classic signet, featuring three lab-grown baguette diamonds set in 14-karat yellow or white gold. The understated design combines the timeless appeal of a signet ring with a sentimental tribute to family, bringing a new perspective to Bird’s growing fine jewelry offering. Available exclusively on Jenny Bird’s website, the collaboration makes a case for jewelry that feels as meaningful as it looks.

Pomellato Revives Its 1997 Moneta Orientale Pendant as a Colorful Talisman

Pomellato is looking to its archives for its latest good-luck charm. For the newest chapter of “Memorie d’Archivio,” the maison revives Moneta Orientale, a 1997 pendant inspired by the ancient symbolism of a circle surrounding a square, representing the harmony between heaven and earth. Made in 33 stone-and-pavé combinations, the design pairs colorful hard stones including black jade, amazonite, sodalite, rhodochrosite, and labradorite with Pomellato’s signature irregular pavé of diamonds, sapphires, rubies, and more. Offered in two proportions, each pendant transforms the archival motif into a modern talisman for prosperity and protection.

Bibi van der Velden Makes Her High Jewelry Debut With ‘Eclipse’

Bibi van der Velden is entering a new era with “Eclipse,” the designer’s first high jewelry collection and most refined exploration of diamonds to date. Inspired by the fleeting moment when light gives way to darkness, the collection includes two six-piece suites: one in white diamonds and another defined by an ombré of diamonds into gray spinels deepening into black. Van der Velden’s signature alligator motif is abstracted into fluid, sculptural silhouettes, with scales engraved into the white gold on the reverse of each piece. “With Eclipse, I wanted to take those familiar elements and transform them into something more abstract and sculptural,” she says. “It’s a collection about transformation, which has always been at the heart of my work.”

Aflalo and Leandra Medine Cohen Turn Everyday Indulgences Into Fine Jewelry

Aflalo is finding the humor in our obsession with wellness with “The Vanities,” a new two-piece fine jewelry capsule designed exclusively by Leandra Medine Cohen. Playing with the contradiction between longevity and life’s little indulgences, the collection transforms two unlikely everyday accessories into precious objects. The Memento Mori is a 14-karat yellow gold cigar band set with more than four carats of diamonds, designed to slip over an Oura Ring, while The Libertine is a sterling silver pendant case adorned with diamonds and a wild-haired woman outlined in gold, designed to hold nicotine pouches or other small essentials. Equal parts extravagant and irreverent, the collection makes a playful case for enjoying life’s pleasures without sacrificing personal style.

Julia Berolzheimer’s Hart Jewelry Collection Draws on Childhood Memories

Hart is teaming up with Julia Berolzheimer for a new jewelry collection that celebrates the art of the stack. Inspired by Berolzheimer’s childhood memories of her grandmother’s California ranch and her collection of Art Deco minaudières, the collaboration brings together whimsical charms, colorful gemstones, and meaningful talismans designed to be mixed, layered, and restyled. Botanical motifs take shape in Tree of Life coins, daisies, bees, and fruit-inspired charms, while carnelian, turquoise, and pink opal add playful pops of color. One standout is the Perfume Vesta Case, a modern interpretation of a Victorian-era accessory that can hold a sample-sized fragrance and hang alongside other charms. With interchangeable chains, cords, and pendants, the collection makes a case for jewelry that feels just as personal as the memories behind it.

David Yurman Captures the Magic of a New York Holiday

David Yurman is celebrating the magic of the holidays in New York City with a new campaign featuring global brand ambassador Michael B. Jordan alongside actresses Yerin Ha and Inde Navarrette. Set against a snow-covered Washington Square Park, the campaign captures a series of quintessential New York moments, from Jordan and Ha facing off in a spirited card game to Navarrette hailing a cab in search of the perfect holiday gift. Throughout the campaign, the cast wears some of the house’s most recognizable designs, including 18-karat gold Cable bracelets and pieces from the “Starburst” and “Armory” collections. Directed by Bradford Young and photographed by Drew Vickers, the campaign brings together the spirit of the city, the joy of togetherness, and the timeless appeal of David Yurman’s jewelry.

Vhernier Reintroduces Its Iconic ‘Trottola’ Design With New Proportions

Vhernier is revisiting one of its most recognizable designs with a new interpretation of “Trottola,” the sculptural collection originally introduced in 2003. Inspired by the continuous motion of a spinning top, the latest designs play with proportions, contrasting materials, and asymmetrical shapes across rings, bracelets, necklaces, and earrings. Polished rose gold meets glossy black jet, with select pieces featuring diamond pavé for an added contrast of light and dark. The collection also focuses on versatility, from rings designed for stacking to convertible earclips that can be worn as studs or dangling earrings. With its fluid forms and unexpected material combinations, “Trottola” brings a fresh perspective to Vhernier’s signature sculptural approach to jewelry.

Di Volpe is rethinking the classic tennis bracelet with “DiSegno,” a new customizable fine jewelry system designed to change with its wearer. Using concealed, patent-pending connections, individual cultured diamonds and gemstones, called Elements, can be removed, rearranged, or added by hand, allowing wearers to transform bracelets into necklaces or earrings without compromising the seamless look of traditional tennis jewelry. The collection launches with 28 stone-and-cut combinations, including rubies, emeralds, sapphires, and diamonds, alongside a limited-edition collaboration with Lebanese artist Ali Cha’aban featuring five sculptural designs. With new cuts, colors, and artist collaborations planned for future releases, “DiSegno” makes the case for fine jewelry that’s never quite finished.

Brent Neale Riffs on the Bow in Fine Jewelry

Brent Neale is putting a bow on the holiday season with “Wrap It Up,” a new fine jewelry collection that transforms the familiar ribbon motif into sculptural works of art. Drawing inspiration from Old Hollywood glamour and the femininity of the 1960s, the designer plays with the contrast between rigid precious metals and the soft movement of fabric, crafting bows that twist, curl, and unfurl in 18-karat gold and platinum. Colored gemstones sit nestled within the ribbon-like forms, while pavé diamonds accentuate every curve and fold. Equal parts playful and precious, the collection brings a little gift-wrapped glamour to the jewelry box.

Grace Winfrey’s ‘Poppy Fortuna’ Collection Reimagines Good-Luck Charms

Grace Winfrey is bringing a little extra luck to the jewelry box with “Poppy Fortuna,” a new fine jewelry collection inspired by the natural beauty of the Italian landscape and symbols of good fortune. Scarlet poppies, sunflowers, bees, four-leaf clovers, horseshoes, and ladybugs come to life through vibrant gemstones and intricate pavé, creating miniature mosaics of color and texture. Highlights include a Lucky Bangle combining three good-luck charms, sculptural sunflower earrings with tiny ladybugs tucked into their petals, and layered charm necklaces designed to feel like modern keepsakes. Handcrafted in New York City, each piece transforms familiar symbols of prosperity, protection, and happiness into playful, colorful works of art.

Robinson Pelham Channels ’90s Glamour for Its Anniversary

Robinson Pelham is closing out its 30th anniversary celebrations with “Suite 96,” a new campaign and collection launch inspired by the glamour of late-’90s London. Set inside a private suite at St. James’s Hotel & Club in Mayfair, the campaign considers jewelry the ultimate room service, with diamonds arriving on trays, gold spilling out of wardrobes, and plenty of pieces to layer before a night out. At the center is “Studio 30,” a four-piece anniversary collection featuring diamond necklaces and statement earrings, including the sculptural Via and Hira necklaces, cascading diamond drops, and the bold Solstice Supreme. Alongside the anniversary designs, the house introduces new collections and additions to existing favorites, from chunky gold links and graphic heart rings to colorful enamel and gemstone combinations. Together, the launches celebrate three decades of Robinson Pelham’s bold, playful approach to fine jewelry.

Le Vian and Jared Revive Georgian-Era Romance

Le Vian is bringing a little old-world romance to Jared Jewelers with its new exclusive “Georgian Chocolate & Nude Diamonds” collection. Inspired by the candlelit jewels of the Georgian era, when jewelry was designed to capture and reflect the warmth of natural light, the collection rethinks historic buttercup settings in polished Honey Gold, with eight rounded prongs framing each natural diamond. The designs pair Le Vian’s signature Chocolate and Nude Diamonds with warm gold detailing across solitaire rings, anniversary bands, tennis bracelets, necklaces, and earrings. Select styles introduce colorful gemstones including Chocolate Quartz, Green Apple Peridot, and Grape Amethyst, giving the vintage-inspired silhouettes a contemporary update. With its sculptural settings and warm-toned stones, the collection brings the romance of antique jewelry into the present.

Wempe’s ‘Au:thentic’ Celebrates the Art of Goldsmithing

Wempe’s new gender-inclusive fine jewelry collection, “Au:thentic,” puts craftsmanship front and center, finding inspiration in the foundational skills taught to aspiring goldsmiths. The collection takes its shape from the jump ring, one of the first techniques Patrick Sieroslawski learned as an apprentice more than 22 years ago, translating its form to necklaces, bracelets, rings, earrings, and pendants. Handcrafted at Wempe’s atelier in Germany, the pieces come in 18-karat yellow, white, and rose gold, with select styles set with diamonds. “Au:thentic” also marks the beginning of a multiyear rollout, with three additional chapters set to expand on its design language through twists, wraps, and interlocking links.

#6648. Phoebe Dynevor Gives a First Look at Her Wedding Ring—and It’s a Timeless Classic

Two months after her marriage to Cameron Fuller, Phoebe Dynevor’s wedding ring has finally been seen out on the town. The actor gave us our first glimpse of the stack on her ring finger while stepping out for coffee in London’s Notting Hill neighborhood—and it proved to be a true classic.

Since her wedding in France this August, Dynevor has worn a simple gold band paired below her gold solitaire oval engagement ring, which features a slender bezel setting. Rather than choosing a style embellished with micro-pavé gemstones or a large eternity ring wrapped with diamonds, the minimal band proves you can let the center stone of your engagement ring do the talking.

Just because the wedding band is simple doesn’t mean Dynevor’s stack is boring, though. Her oval-cut diamond likely sits around three carats, taking up some major real estate on the Bridgerton star’s slender finger. And while the gold band isn’t flashy, the way it pairs with her ring makes it feel modern. Since the diamond on her engagement ring has a low-profile setting, it makes it difficult for another band to sit flush beneath the stone. So rather than tucking underneath the diamond, the band rests at the edge of the stone and leaves some negative space free on Dynevor’s finger. Paired with the engagement ring’s bezel setting—which also offers protection to the diamond—the two rings together lend the stone a floating effect.

Dynevor isn’t the only famous bride who has opted for a simpler gold wedding band as of late. Zendaya and her new husband Tom Holland have each stepped out wearing the minimal ring style since their nuptials, and Anne Hathaway also wears one underneath her large emerald-cut diamond engagement ring. As thicker bands and unique settings have become trendier for engagement rings this past year, we’ve also seen many couples choosing to stick with gold bands to balance out these styles.

The style is a classic for a reason. First, the timeless band remains true to the original symbolism of a wedding ring, whose circular shape represents eternity, unbroken commitment, and mutual fidelity. It’s also an excellent choice for those who lean towards practicality. A simple gold band requires very little maintenance, doesn’t risk losing any stones from improper care, and is easy to wear at all times without needing to remove it. Many people also choose to have gold bands as a spacer ring, which can be worn alongside a more elaborate eternity band given for an anniversary gift or push present down the line.

Engagement and wedding ring trends have changed dramatically in recent years. Lab-grown diamonds are now so popular that many to-be-weds have been looking towards bold styles to stand out, from modern, off-center settings to colorful gemstones and antique jewelry pieces. Phoebe Dynevor’s wedding ring might be a sign that amid the search for originality, you shouldn’t ignore the classics.

#6647. Sade Is No Ordinary Style Icon

An ode to the singer who was ahead of her time.

Has there ever been anyone as effortlessly ahead of her time as Sade? Born Helen Folasade Adu on Jan. 16, 1959, in Ibadan, Nigeria, the frontwoman of her namesake band has a core aesthetic that revolves around blindingly bright hoop earrings, a slicked-back bun, a deep red lip, and strong yet minimal silhouettes. As the band is inducted into the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame this weekend, there’s never been a better time to reflect on the British-Nigerian singer’s personal style. Think: sweaters with strong shoulders, thick belts on long cinched skirts, and, when called for, a perfectly eccentric evening jacket souped up with embroidery and satisfyingly present buttons.

Chalk it up to her era; Sade exploded in popularity in the ’80s, when these kinds of powerful silhouettes reigned supreme, but even beyond that, she knew the power of style. And it’s no wonder: Years ago, in a rare radio interview, she divulged that fashion was her passion long before music. “I made clothes. For three years I went to an art college and did fashion at Central Saint Martins in London,” she said. “I actually sold clothes, and that’s when I started to sing. I had to make a choice between doing the two, because I didn’t have enough time.” Though her foray into design was incredibly sparsely documented, her focus was on menswear, and she later co-founded the tailored menswear fashion label Demob with designer Sarah Lee, where the duo created club-kid-ready attire.

Onstage, whether she was singing “Smooth Operator” or “No Ordinary Love,” she wore her finishing touches with pride: lush little leather gloves in olive green to match a soft-shouldered woolen suit, or a festooning delicate statement necklace layered over a black tank top. Rather than layer multiple pieces, she communicates through the subtle impact of one-and-done statements. A delicate stack of bracelets, or modernist front-facing Lucite hoop earrings, for instance. She usually leans into white and black, except for the rare occasion when she chooses a jammy, rich shade of plum or deep olive green. Her attention to detail does not go unnoticed; there’s a clear knack for tailored silhouettes.

Sade’s elusive nature combined with the ethereal sound of her music also contributes to fashion forming her memorable identity. Long before others made a plain turtleneck or slicked-back hairstyle their uniform, there was Sade doing it authentically, and with accessorized flair. And in today’s era of highly produced musicians who are styled by a team, Sade still stands out.

Though Sade and her band will not be present at the ceremony, they called it “both a gift and a timely reminder to give thanks, not only to those who voted for us but also every single person who lets our music into their lives” in a statement. For every person who’s ever loved an accessory and a bold shoulder look (especially gold hoop earrings), Sade’s presence lives on beyond the music too.

#6644. Maple Bourbon Chicken With Brussels Sprouts

If you, like most people, hear the term “bourbon chicken” and have no idea what it is, let me call it by its more common name: toothpick chicken. Yes, the suspiciously delicious chicken shelled out at mall food courts on toothpicks is most likely bourbon chicken. Popular at American Chinese or Cajun-style Chinese restaurants, the sticky-sweet chicken is the utter definition of delicious, luring weary shoppers into food courts to find refuge from the bubblegum pink sweatpants and ripped denim. This version takes cues from the classic but swaps in some autumnal ingredients to make it fit for the season. Charred brussels sprouts leaves and pecans add bulk, while maple syrup and apple cider vinegar give it that delightful tart-sweet flavor we know and love. Serve it over rice or noodles or all by its lonesome for a hearty dinner that will take you back to the '90s.

More chicken dinner winners here: Sheet-Pan Hot Honey Chicken and Peaches; Basil Chicken Stir-Fry; and Ginger-Garlic Chicken and Vegetable Stir-Fry.

Whisk one 1½" piece ginger, peeled, finely grated, 3 garlic cloves, finely chopped, ⅓ cup bourbon, ⅓ cup pure maple syrup, ¼ cup apple cider vinegar, ¼ tsp. crushed red pepper flakes, 1 Tbsp. cornstarch, ¼ cup low-sodium soy sauce, and ½ cup water in a small bowl to combine. Set sauce aside.

Toss 1½ lb. skinless, boneless chicken breasts, halved crosswise, thinly sliced against the grain, remaining 1 Tbsp. cornstarch, and remaining 1 Tbsp. low-sodium soy sauce in a medium bowl until chicken is coated; set aside.

Heat 2 Tbsp. vegetable oil in a large skillet over medium-high. Add 1 lb. brussels sprouts, halved through stems, leaves separated, and cook, stirring very occasionally, until just tender and blackened in spots, about 5 minutes. Transfer to another medium bowl.

Add more oil if pan looks dry and, working in batches if needed, arrange reserved chicken in a single layer and cook, turning occasionally, until golden brown and cooked through, about 5 minutes. Transfer to bowl with brussels sprouts.

Add reserved sauce to same pan and bring to a simmer. Cook, stirring constantly, until thickened, about 1 minute. Remove pan from heat and return brussels sprouts and chicken to pan; top with 1 cup salted roasted pecans, coarsely chopped. Toss to coat in sauce. Serve chicken and brussels sprouts with steamed white rice if desired.
